What does this cost, and how do you get paid?
We sell no equipment and take no referral fees. Our fee is a retainer plus a share of verified results. Coach and specialist time is passed through at cost. We only earn more when you save more.
What do we get if we stop after the Diagnostic?

Everything the Diagnostic produced is yours to keep: an initial baseline built from your available data, the opportunity map, and the one action that stands out with the numbers behind it. There is no lock-in. If you take the plan and execute it yourself or with another partner, you still leave with a clearer decision.
What happens after the first call?

The call is 30 minutes with a principal. We clarify the decision and tell you if there is likely a material opportunity. Next comes a situation assessment, data collection starts, and we identify low-risk first wins that can be proven with the data on hand. Ongoing work is a steady series of initiatives reported in dollars saved and environmental results.

The CFO usually hires us. Operations, facilities, procurement and sustainability leaders weigh in on recommendations that affect them. We bring the right people in for each one. The outcome is better financial performance first, better sustainability performance close behind, with both reported continuously.
How much of our team's time will this take?

Less than you would expect. The heaviest lift is data access at the start: utility bills, operational records, and whatever environmental reporting you already have. After that, we do the analysis and come back to you with decisions, not homework. During implementation, your named Coach coordinates vendors and specialists so your team is not running another project on the side of their day jobs.

We are not a large enterprise. Is this still for us?

The approach scales down as well as up. Start with one operating group or one cost category across the business. The logic is the same at any size: establish the baseline, rank the opportunities, act on the strongest one, and let the results fund what comes next.
How quickly will we see results?

It depends on the opportunity that ranks first, and we will not pretend otherwise. Some actions, such as rate structures, incentive capture and operational adjustments, can show results within months. Capital projects take longer. Speed is central to the model because the value comes from implementing the right sequence of projects, not from a single promise.
How do we know the savings are real and not consultant math?

Not on its own, and neither do we. First, actio helps screen out what is not material and identify the next best move from the available data. What data do you need from us to get started?

Whatever you have. Utility bills, fuel and fleet records, waste invoices, building and equipment inventories, and prior audits or reports are useful starting points. We start where the data or funding already exists, identify the gaps that matter to the decision, and collect more only when it changes the answer. Each completed action improves the next decision.
We are not going to hand over a mountain of data up front.

You do not have to. Nobody has complete data on day one and we do not build the plan on the assumption that you do. We start with the available data, look for low-risk early wins, and prioritize only the collection work that can make the next answer sharper. Every result earns the next piece of access.
What happens if we do not have good data?

You do not need a complete global data set before you begin. We start with the available data or funding path, take the quick wins first, and use the results to earn access to better data. The whole-field program comes later, once the data has compounded.

We already know what our biggest opportunity is?

You may be right. In our experience the answer is usually somewhere the organization was not looking, because the obvious candidate is obvious to everyone including your vendors, and it has usually been priced accordingly. We do not arrive with a view either. The first engagement exists to find out, against your data and the whole field, rather than to confirm what either of us assumed.
Do you only work on buildings and energy?

No. Energy in buildings is often where the data is richest, but the playing field is much wider. Fleet and fuel switching, water, waste, supply chain, procurement, and sector-specific opportunities. The right starting point differs by organization. A municipality's priorities are not a manufacturer's, and a farm's are not a REIT's. That is exactly why we start wide. The bigger the field we search, the more likely your best opportunity is the true maximum, not just the best of a narrow list.
Why does our location matter to the analysis?

Because the same project produces different returns in different places. Utility and government funding programs, energy rates, insurance costs, and operating conditions all vary by jurisdiction, and they materially change payback. Higher energy rates make efficiency savings worth more; available incentives can transform a marginal project into a compelling one. Jurisdictional intelligence is one of the three pillars of our analysis, alongside your operational data and our vendor market data.
We mostly care about the financial return. Is that a problem?

Not at all. It is how we are built. A solution is only considered by us if it has a positive environmental impact and provides a financial return; within that field, we rank by overall business case. You never have to choose between an initiative that pays and an initiative that helps. The ones we recommend do both, and the business case is designed to survive policy changes.
Can you help us with climate risk, not just cost savings?

Yes, and it is a growing part of the work. Interconnected environmental pressures, including wildfires, flooding, drought, and supply chain disruption, are already showing up in insurance availability, input costs, and asset values. We help clients think strategically about exposure: where operations are located, how supply chains can be shortened, and which risks deserve action now. The same discipline applies: rank the exposures, act on the material ones first.

audiencePage.heroBody: Climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution now show up as fuel cost, input volatility, disrupted supply chains and capital decisions that do not clear your hurdle rate. There are thousands of credible solutions, but a finance team should not have to work out which one belongs in the capital plan. That is the gap we close.

audiencePage.polycrisisTitle: Three interlocking pressures, not one. Each reaches the business through a different line.
audiencePage.polycrisisIntro: Polycrisis is a precise term. Climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution reinforce one another, which is why separate files, budgets and vendor proposals rarely produce a coherent capital decision.

pressures.title: Climate change
pressures.body: Extreme weather across your sites and suppliers, volatile energy costs, physical risk to fixed assets and unplanned downtime.

pressures.title: Biodiversity loss
pressures.body: Input security where raw materials depend on soil, water, pollination or fisheries, with costs rising before regulation arrives.

pressures.title: Pollution and waste
pressures.body: Waste, effluent, air quality and refrigerant exposure, increasingly carried through customer and supply-chain requirements.

audiencePage.compoundingNote: A drought can become a water-availability issue, then an input-cost issue, then a supply-contract issue. We screen the connected problem against one set of financial criteria.
audiencePage.decisionTitle: The market has produced an abundance of credible options. That abundance is the barrier.
decisionBody: Technologies, service providers, funding programs and software platforms each solve part of the problem. Many are competent. Most are designed to begin from the solution they sell.
Your decision is not whether an option is plausible. It is whether it is the best next use of capital for your organization, compared with the alternatives you have not yet seen.
That comparison is a technical screening exercise. We do the screening, name the one initiative worth funding next, and see it through with the right partners. Then we do it again at speed.

realityItems.title: Does it work on our criterion?

audiencePage.heroBody: Flooding, wildfire, heat and storm damage now land directly on municipal assets and municipal budgets. There are credible responses, competing funding windows and a capital plan that cannot hold every project. We help identify which line belongs first, what evidence it needs and how to frame it for council.

trustExamples.title: The project needs to survive the public meeting.

audiencePage.polycrisisTitle: Three interlocking pressures, not one. Each lands on a different part of the capital plan.
audiencePage.polycrisisIntro: For municipalities, the environmental polycrisis is an asset-management problem. It affects the condition, service level, replacement timing and funding requirements of the infrastructure you already own.

pressures.title: Climate change
pressures.body: Stormwater systems sized for old rainfall patterns, flood and wildfire damage, heat loads on facilities and shortened service life for roads and pipe.

pressures.title: Biodiversity loss
pressures.body: Natural assets such as wetlands, tree canopy and watercourses that perform retention and cooling work otherwise carried by built capital.

pressures.title: Pollution and waste
pressures.body: Drinking-water treatment, wastewater, landfill capacity, contaminated sites and air quality during smoke events.

audiencePage.compoundingNote: A degraded wetland can raise the stormwater requirement, which competes with water treatment and roads renewal in the same budget. The decision needs one set of financial and service-level criteria.
audiencePage.decisionTitle: Municipal staff are asked to solve connected asset problems one grant application at a time.
decisionBody: Funding programs, condition assessments, feasibility studies and procurement cycles do not arrive on the same schedule. A good project can still miss its moment if the evidence was not prepared before the window opened.
We start with the assets, studies and operating information you already hold. Then we determine which gaps matter, which funding routes are worth pursuing and what the capital plan should do first.
The work is framed as asset renewal, avoided cost, level of service and lifecycle value, because that is the language a public capital decision must survive in.
audiencePage.realityTitle: What the work must make clear
audiencePage.realityIntro: The report should answer the questions staff and council actually need answered.

realityItems.title: What is the cost of continuing to defer?
realityItems.body: We make the service, operating and lifecycle implications visible, rather than treating the project as a standalone environmental initiative.

realityItems.title: What evidence is needed before a funding application?
realityItems.body: We identify the condition, feasibility, audit or assessment work needed to make an application credible, and whether that preparatory work is itself fundable.

realityItems.title: How does this affect reserves and the levy?
realityItems.body: Recommendations are presented in the units council debates: capital, operating cost, reserves, service level and timing.

audiencePage.howItStartsTitle: Start with your portfolio and the decision you are trying to make.

audiencePage.heroBody: Wildfire, flooding, water quality and the cost of diesel are not abstract in your community. We work for the Nation, on the Nation’s terms, to identify what should be done first, see it delivered, and reassess for the next one at speed.

trustExamples.title: The question is not only what to build, but what remains with the Nation.

trustExamples.title: The first result should improve the next decision.

audiencePage.polycrisisTitle: Three pressures at once, not one. Your community will have seen all three before we describe them.
audiencePage.polycrisisIntro: We use polycrisis to mean climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution happening together. This is our working definition, not an attempt to explain the land to the people who know it.

pressures.title: Climate change
pressures.body: Evacuations and smoke seasons, flooding, shorter winter-road seasons, thawing ground and shifting timing for harvest, fishery and travel.

pressures.title: Biodiversity loss
pressures.body: Changes to fish, game, plants and water connected to food, medicine, culture, income and community wellbeing.

pressures.title: Pollution and waste
pressures.body: Drinking-water quality, contaminated sites, waste handling and the particulate and cost burden associated with diesel generation.

audiencePage.compoundingNote: Funding categories separate what the community experiences together. Adaptation, clean energy, water and housing may arrive through different systems, even when one project could address more than one priority.
audiencePage.decisionKicker: What a long-term partner means in practice
audiencePage.decisionTitle: The work has to be accountable to council, useful to staff and capable of surviving an election.
decisionBody: Authority needs to rest with council and the community process the Nation uses, not a personal relationship with one leader. The work should be documented so an incoming council can understand what was decided and why.
We begin with the records the Nation already holds, often including condition information, utility records and lifecycle material. A complete data set is not a precondition for beginning.
Where ownership, revenue and control can remain with the Nation, that is the structure to pursue. Capacity should be transferred, not turned into dependency on an advisor.

realityItems.title: Council authority and a clear record
realityItems.body: The work is anchored in the Nation’s governance and written so decisions, assumptions and next steps remain clear over time.

realityItems.title: Ownership and capacity
realityItems.body: The goal is for Nation staff to understand the method, retain the documentation and lead future cycles with less external support.

realityItems.title: Commercial clarity
realityItems.body: Scope and terms are agreed before work begins. We sell no equipment and take no supplier referral fees.

audiencePage.heroTitle: You feel the polycrisis before anyone else does. Sorting through the programs and the salesmen is not your job.
audiencePage.heroBody: Drought, fire, flood and heat show up in yield and input bills first. audiencePage.trustIntro: These are representative on-farm questions, not claims about client results. The decision is tested against the operation in front of us, not a brochure or a generic average.

trustExamples.title: The reimbursement looks attractive, until the cash timing is visible.
trustExamples.body: Test eligibility, timing, sign-offs and the amount carried by the operation before money arrives.

trustExamples.title: A carbon or environmental contract deserves the same scrutiny as any long-term commitment.
trustExamples.body: Read the economics, obligations, permanence terms, fees and exit conditions before deciding whether the offer clears on your ground.

trustExamples.title: The right machine or system still has to earn its place.
trustExamples.body: Compare operating fit, existing equipment, fuel or utility exposure and practical timing before committing capital.

audiencePage.polycrisisTitle: Three pressures at once, not one. You are on the receiving end of all three.
audiencePage.polycrisisIntro: Polycrisis is a practical way to describe climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution happening together. On a farm, the effects meet in the same margin calculation.

pressures.title: Climate change
pressures.body: Drought, heat during grain fill, hail, flooding and changing seeding and harvest windows that reduce room for error.

pressures.title: Biodiversity loss
pressures.body: Pollinators, beneficial insects and soil biology. When these decline, yield becomes harder to hold and purchased inputs may rise.

pressures.title: Pollution and waste
pressures.body: Nutrient runoff, water quality requirements and buyer expectations that increasingly affect market access.

audiencePage.compoundingNote: Drought can stress soil biology, weaker soil biology can increase input dependency, and higher input use can raise both cost and runoff exposure. The margin does not care which program owns each piece.
audiencePage.decisionTitle: Thousands of offers may work somewhere. That does not mean they clear on your ground.
decisionBody: Equipment, inputs, carbon arrangements and incentive programs are often presented as a simple yes-or-no decision. They are not. The details of your acres, cash flow, timing and existing equipment change the answer.
We do not sell equipment, inputs or carbon contracts, and we take no referral fees. That gives us room to say when a program, contract or purchase does not clear the economic hurdle.
The work is to identify the one next action worth making, deliver it, reassess, and name the next one. At speed, because the field keeps moving while you decide.
audiencePage.realityTitle: What the recommendation needs to show
audiencePage.realityIntro: Straight answers, in the units that matter on the operation.

realityItems.title: Out-of-pocket exposure
realityItems.body: A reimbursement program is a cash-flow decision before it is an environmental one. We consider timing and financing, not just the headline funding amount.

realityItems.title: Per-acre or per-unit economics
realityItems.body: You receive the numbers behind the recommendation, including the likely return, practical constraints and what would need to be true for it to work.

realityItems.title: Contract terms
realityItems.body: Long commitments, permanence clauses, fees and penalties deserve a clear reading before any carbon or program contract is signed.

audiencePage.howItStartsTitle: Bring the decision you keep pushing to next year.

pressures.title: Climate change
pressures.body: Flood exposure by asset location, cooling load, storm damage, business interruption and building-specific insurability.

pressures.title: Biodiversity loss
pressures.body: Land use, stormwater and green-infrastructure requirements, redevelopment friction and site-level nature exposure.

pressures.title: Pollution and waste
pressures.body: Wildfire smoke ingress, indoor air quality, refrigerant transitions, tenant obligations and contaminated land at disposition or redevelopment.

audiencePage.decisionKicker: Why choosing is the hard part
audiencePage.decisionTitle: The retrofit case has to stand on economics, not on an assumption that a mandate or incentive will carry it.

realityItems.title: Does it fit the hold period and recovery position?
realityItems.body: The hold period, base-building versus tenant scope and actual lease permissions change the ranking. They are inputs, not afterthoughts.

sections.content:
After 45 years working in energy, I look at climate change through a fairly simple lens.

Energy has to go somewhere.

If more energy enters a system than leaves it, the difference builds up. That is what is happening to the Earth today. Greenhouse gases have changed the planet’s energy balance, and most of the extra heat is ending up in one place.

Not the atmosphere. The oceans.

More than 90 per cent of the extra heat building up in the climate system is stored in the ocean. The atmosphere holds only a small fraction. [1]

That makes ocean heat content one of the most useful measures we have of what is really happening to the climate. It is also one of the least discussed.
The numbers are getting hard to ignore

In 2025, the heat stored in the top 2,000 metres of the global ocean reached the highest level since records began in 1960. Each of the past nine years has set a new record. [2]

The pace matters even more than the record. The ocean warmed more than twice as fast from 2005 to 2025 as it did from 1960 to 2005. [2]

The World Meteorological Organization puts the recent build up at about 11 to 12.2 zettajoules a year. [2]

A zettajoule is so large it is hard to picture. Try this. Each year the ocean is taking on heat equal to about 18 times all the energy humanity uses. [2]

I have spent my career working with energy numbers. Eighteen times global energy use is not a rounding error. It is a staggering amount of energy.
Why the oceans

Water is extremely good at absorbing and storing heat. That is one reason the oceans have mitigated the warming we feel on land and in the air.

But the heat has not gone away. It has been stored somewhere else.

Burning fossil fuels, industry and cutting forests all add carbon dioxide, methane and other greenhouse gases to the air. As they build up, less heat escapes to space. The planet takes in more energy than it gives off. The ocean absorbs most of the difference. [3, 9]
El Niño, La Niña and the super El Niño now forming

Any discussion of ocean heat has to deal with El Niño and La Niña. They drive most of the ups and downs in global temperature from one year to the next.

I find it helps to think of them as the Pacific Ocean’s heat valve.

During La Niña, strong trade winds push warm surface water west toward Asia. Cold water rises in the eastern Pacific. More heat gets tucked below the surface, and global temperatures dip for a while.

During El Niño, those winds weaken. Warm water spreads east across the surface of the Pacific and gives up heat to the air. Global temperatures jump.

Neither one adds heat to the planet. They move heat between the ocean and the air. The long climb in ocean heat comes from the energy imbalance, not from these cycles. That build up tracks the rise in greenhouse gases. [9, 10]

2025 showed this well. La Niña cooled the planet for a while, and 2025 ended up the second or third warmest year on record rather than the warmest. Ocean heat content still set a new record. [2]
The valve is now swinging hard the other way

La Niña faded early in 2026. El Niño then formed over the summer and is building fast.

On September 10, the NOAA said there is a greater than 90 per cent chance of a very strong El Niño this fall and winter. It gives a 75 per cent chance that, from October to December, this event will be stronger than any El Niño since 1950. [12] That is what people mean by a super El Niño.

We can already see it. August 2026 tied July 2023 as the warmest month ever recorded, at about 1.65°C above pre‑industrial levels. The global average sea surface temperature hit a daily record of 21.11°C. [13]

Satellites watch the ocean surface every day. The people who run them say this El Niño has surprised many experts with its strength. [16]
What it means

This El Niño is arriving on top of the most heat the ocean has ever held. That combination is new.

Strong El Niños have set global temperature records before. 1998 and 2016 both did. Canadian climate scientists now expect 2027 to break the record set in 2024. [14]

For Canada, a strong El Niño usually means a milder winter across much of the country. That lowers heating demand. It also tends to mean less snow in the Rockies, BC and Alberta. Less snowpack means less water for hydro dams, cities and farms next year. The same pattern raises the risk of spring drought in grain regions and a bigger wildfire season. Freezing rain events can hit transport and power lines. [14]

Around the world, El Niño tends to dry out Indonesia and Australia and weaken India’s monsoon. It can hurt cocoa and other crops. It usually means fewer Atlantic hurricanes, because it strengthens the winds that tear storms apart. [15] That fits the point I make below. The number of storms is not the real measure.

There is one more thing to watch. As El Niño pulls heat out of the ocean and into the air, upper ocean heat readings may level off or dip for a while. That will not mean the problem is easing. It will mean stored heat is coming back to the surface.

In energy terms, El Niño is a withdrawal from storage. The deposits keep coming. When this event fades, the build up will continue from a higher starting point.

For anyone running buildings, utilities or supply chains, the lesson is simple. Plan for a year of extremes. A mild winter in Ontario is not a sign the climate is calming down.
What that much extra energy does
The effects go well beyond slightly warmer water.
Sea levels rise

Warm water expands. It is basic physics.

Thermal expansion and melting glaciers and ice sheets both raise sea levels. The IPCC found that expansion caused about half of sea level rise from 1971 to 2018. Melting land ice became the bigger driver from 2006 to 2018. [1]

By 2025, global average sea level was about 11 centimetres higher than when satellite measurements began in 1993. [2]

As with atmospheric and ocean temperatures, the rate of sea level rise is speeding up too. Satellites now show sea level climbing about 4 millimetres a year, up from about 3 millimetres a year over the previous two decades. [16]

For coastal towns, ports, infrastructure and property owners, centimetres matter.
Storms have more energy to draw on

Here we need to be careful with the words.

Warmer oceans do not mean more hurricanes. Research suggests the total number of tropical cyclones may stay about the same or even fall.

What warmer water does is give the storms that do form more energy and more moisture. Research assessed by NOAA indicates warming is expected to bring heavier rainfall from these storms and a larger share of the most intense ones. Higher seas make storm surge more damaging as well. [4]

So the question is not how many storms we get. It is what those storms can do.
Marine heatwaves are more common

A marine heatwave is the ocean version of a long heatwave on land.

The IPCC found they have roughly doubled in frequency since the 1980s. They have grown more intense and last longer. [5]

In 2025, about 90 per cent of the ocean surface had at least one marine heatwave. [2]

That number stands out. Ocean life evolved within set temperature ranges. Push past them far enough, or long enough, and these ranges start to change.
Fish move

Fish do not follow provincial lines, national borders or fishery zones. They follow habitat.

As water warms, many species are moving toward cooler water, often north or deeper. NOAA already tracks changes in where commercially important species are found. That affects fishing fleets, coastal economies and how fisheries are managed. [6]

Many coastal communities, including Indigenous communities, have relied on the same species for generations. When stocks shift, it is more than a business loss. It can put food security and long held ties to the sea at risk. [10]

An environmental issue quickly becomes an economic one. Fishing, tourism and coastal jobs support millions of people worldwide.
Reefs and ecosystems come under stress

Coral bleaching is the most visible sign of an ocean that is too warm. When the heat lasts, bleached coral can die across large parts of a reef. The larger issue is disruption across whole ecosystems.

Temperature affects where species live, when they breed, what they eat and which predators and rivals they meet. When those links change, whole food webs can change with them.

Ocean warming is already linked to damaged marine ecosystems, loss of biodiversity and a weaker ocean carbon sink. [2]
The ocean has been protecting us

There is an irony here that often gets missed.

By soaking up most of the extra heat, the oceans have shielded us from much faster warming in the air.

But there is no free storage.

That energy shows up somewhere. It shows up in rising seas, marine heatwaves, shifting fisheries, stressed ecosystems, melting ice and the extra fuel available to strong storms.
What we do with that knowledge

The physics is not controversial. If greenhouse gases keep building up, extra energy will keep building up in the climate system. Most of it will keep going into the ocean.

Cutting emissions slows how fast that energy builds up. But the heat already stored in the ocean means adaptation is no longer optional. The deep ocean responds slowly, so some ocean warming and sea level rise will last for centuries. [5]

For decision makers, that points in two directions at once. Cut emissions to slow the build up. Increase adaptability and resilience by planning assets, supply chains and coastal operations for a future where certain conditions are already locked in.

sections.content:
Greenhouse gas concentrations are now rising at a rate unprecedented in human civilization and many times faster than at almost any point in the geological record. The cause is well established. Human activity, principally the combustion of fossil fuels together with industrial processes, agriculture and land use change, is releasing vast quantities of carbon dioxide, methane and other greenhouse gases. Past greenhouse gas emission and associated temperature increases unfolded over thousands of years. Modern emissions and temperatures have risen within a few decades, far faster than the natural systems that regulate atmospheric carbon and temperatures can respond. [8]

This is key. It is not the absolute level of current temperatures that most concerns scientists. Temperatures have been higher in the past. Rather it is the rate that temperatures are increasing and our ability to adapt to them that worries scientists most.

After more than four decades in energy, I have learned that the most consequential risks are often the ones that build steadily in the background. Climate change is one of them. Warming has accelerated, and the reasons behind that acceleration matter to anyone making long term decisions about buildings, equipment and energy infrastructure.
Emissions keep accumulating

The continued use of coal, oil and natural gas remains the largest contributor. Renewable energy is growing rapidly, and the International Energy Agency reports that growth in global energy related carbon dioxide emissions slowed to about 0.4 per cent in 2025. Yet demand for all three fossil fuels still increased, and the world continues to add tens of billions of tonnes of carbon dioxide to the atmosphere each year. [2]

Because carbon dioxide can persist in the atmosphere for centuries, each year's emissions are added to the accumulation from previous years. That continuing buildup strengthens the greenhouse effect and increases the heat retained within the Earth system. Slower growth in emissions is welcome, but it does not stop the accumulation. Only reaching net zero does. [3, 8]
Cleaner air has removed a temporary shield

An additional factor accelerating warming is the reduction of aerosol pollution. Sulfate aerosols produced by fossil fuel combustion and other industrial activity reflect sunlight back into space and help form brighter clouds, creating a temporary cooling effect. Air quality regulations have successfully lowered these emissions in many regions, with major benefits for public health. They have also removed part of the mask over greenhouse gas warming.

The most recent assessment estimates that human induced warming reached about 0.27°C per decade over 2016 to 2025, faster than in earlier decades. That acceleration reflects both high greenhouse gas emissions and reduced aerosol cooling. [1] The lesson is not to tolerate harmful pollution. It is that any serious energy strategy must account for the full physics of the transition.
Natural carbon sinks are under strain

Forests, oceans, soils, and wetlands have absorbed roughly half of human carbon dioxide emissions and have done a great deal to moderate climate change. [3, 4] Rising temperatures, drought, pest infestations and wildfire are now reducing the capacity of many forests to absorb carbon. In some regions and years, forests hit by fire or drought have released more carbon than they took up. The oceans have absorbed most of the excess heat generated by greenhouse gases and a substantial portion of emitted carbon dioxide. [5] Warmer water, however, holds less carbon dioxide than colder water, which reduces the effectiveness of one of Earth's largest carbon sinks. Warmer oceans also contribute to changes in circulation that affect how heat and carbon move through the climate system. [3, 4, 5]

These natural sinks still absorb substantial amounts of carbon, and their performance varies from year to year. The concern is that climate change has already reduced their uptake compared with what it would have been without that warming. As they weaken, a larger share of every tonne emitted stays in the atmosphere. [4]
Shrinking ice and snow amplify warming

Ice sheets, sea ice and snow reflect a large proportion of incoming sunlight through the albedo effect. As warming causes these surfaces to shrink, darker land and ocean are exposed. Those darker surfaces absorb more sunlight, producing additional warming that leads to further melting. This reinforcing feedback loop is especially strong in the Arctic, where temperatures are rising several times faster than the global average. [6]
Thawing permafrost releases more greenhouse gases

Vast areas of permanently frozen ground in northern regions hold enormous stores of organic carbon accumulated over thousands of years. As permafrost thaws, microbes break down this material and release carbon dioxide and methane. Methane is particularly significant because it traps far more heat than carbon dioxide over shorter periods. Warming therefore leads to additional emissions, which in turn lead to more warming, another dangerous reinforcing feedback loop. [7]
Deforestation intensifies the cycle

When forests are cleared or burned, the carbon stored in trees and soils is released into the atmosphere, and the capacity of those forests to absorb future emissions is lost. Large scale forest loss in tropical regions, combined with increasing wildfire activity in many parts of the world, means both more emissions and less carbon removal. [4]
A system that is becoming less forgiving

Global temperatures are accelerating because human greenhouse gas emissions remain high while several natural feedback loops amplify their effect. Continued fossil fuel use, reduced cooling from aerosols, weakening carbon sinks, warming oceans, declining ice and snow, methane from thawing permafrost and ongoing deforestation are all acting in the same direction. The size and timing of each feedback differs. Together they create a self reinforcing cycle in which rising temperatures trigger processes that cause still more warming. [1, 4, 8]

None of these feedbacks changes the fundamental cause of rising temperatures, which is continued human emissions. The IPCC is clear that limiting warming requires reaching net zero carbon dioxide emissions alongside deep reductions in other greenhouse gases, and that the total emitted before reaching that point matters. [8] Our choices continue to determine how much additional warming occurs.
What this means for decision makers

As warming gets faster and faster, pressure will build on organizations to react. Decision makers can expect greatly increased focus on their decarbonization performance. It will come from governments, investors, employees and customers, and continuing global warming and its increasingly severe consequences will add to it. Expect increased compliance pressure too. We are nearing a tipping point. We either act or we suffer the consequences. The pendulum has swung far away from taking serious action on climate change and other major environmental issues, especially in the US. Look for it to swing back hard.

For those responsible for buildings, industrial equipment and energy infrastructure, this evidence of global warming speeding up belongs in the next capital budget, the next equipment replacement and the next infrastructure plan. Solutions implemented today will operate for decades under conditions that are changing faster than many plans assume. They need to be judged on how they will perform under those conditions, both in terms of their environmental consequences and their financial impact.
How Enduring Advantage can help

The order and the speed at which solutions are put in place matters. That is especially true for the projects that make a material difference to environmental and financial results.

We use evidence to find the right things to do, in the right order, with the right vendors. Then we ensure implement occurs, and we measure the impact. The outcome is much stronger environmental and financial performance over time.

Faster warming leaves less room for error. Organizations must respond. The advantage goes to leaders who act on evidence, get the order right, move quickly and measure what they get.

This is a consequential time to be a buyer of sustainability solutions. There are many capable products, services, and software platforms available to enterprise buyers. The customer’s problem is not scarcity. It is too many options, too much complexity, and too little clarity about which ones actually move the needle on the corporate bottom line.

Companies that treat sustainability as a financial performance discipline, not a reporting function, consistently outperform their peers on operating margin, cost of capital, and asset utilisation. The mechanism is not mysterious. Sustainability, properly measured, is a proxy for operational efficiency. Energy waste is financial waste. Water inefficiency is procurement inefficiency. Supply chain carbon exposure is supply chain concentration risk. These are not environmental abstractions. They are line items.
The companies that unlock the most value from sustainability are not the ones with the largest programs. They are the ones with the clearest view of which actions to take next.
The Measurement Problem

The reason most sustainability programs fail to deliver financial returns is not ambition. It is measurement. Specifically, it is the absence of a method for screening candidate initiatives by financial return and identifying the one action that stands above the rest for the CFO.

Most enterprise sustainability programs are tracking between 200 and 600 candidate initiatives at any given time. The typical prioritisation method is a combination of stakeholder visibility, ease of implementation, and alignment with disclosure frameworks. These are not financial criteria. They are political criteria. And they systematically deprioritise the highest-value opportunities in favour of the most visible ones.

The result is a program that looks productive, initiatives are being completed, disclosures are improving, ESG scores are moving, but is not delivering the financial returns that would justify its budget. The CFO eventually asks the question that ends the program: what is this actually worth?
What Changes When You Treat It as Finance

The shift is not philosophical. It is methodological. When a sustainability program is run as a financial performance discipline, three things change immediately.

First, candidate initiatives are scored on a common financial metric: projected annual savings, payback period, and GHG reduction per dollar invested. This identifies the one action that stands out, which the CFO can interrogate, challenge, and act on. The conversation changes from "here is what we are doing" to "here is what this is worth."

Second, the baseline becomes auditable. The starting point for every initiative is a verified data baseline, not a self-reported estimate, not a consultant's assumption, but a quality-controlled dataset that can be independently verified and incorporated into financial reporting. This matters enormously when sustainability-linked financing is on the table, because lenders and investors require exactly this kind of auditability.

faq.question: What is the green financing gap?
faq.answer: The green financing gap is the difference between the trillions of dollars in sustainability-linked capital available to enterprise borrowers and the small fraction that companies actually access. The barrier is not ambition, it is the absence of audit-ready environmental data that lenders require before pricing sustainability-linked instruments.

faq.question: What do lenders require to issue a sustainability-linked loan?
faq.answer: Lenders require a quality-controlled, independently verifiable baseline dataset that establishes where the company actually is today on key metrics such as Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions, energy intensity, and waste diversion rates. Self-reported estimates or disclosure-grade data are not sufficient, the baseline must be audit-ready.

faq.answer: Qualifying borrowers typically receive a pricing advantage of 15 to 50 basis points on the coupon. For a company carrying $200 million in long-term debt, a 30-basis-point improvement is $600,000 per year in reduced interest expense, a material cost-of-capital improvement that compounds over the life of the facility.

faq.question: How long does it take to build an audit-ready sustainability baseline?
faq.answer: The timeline depends on the complexity of the business and the current state of its data. For a mid-market company with 10–20 facilities, Enduring Advantage typically completes a financing-grade baseline in 8–16 weeks. The cost of building the baseline is typically recovered within months through the interest rate savings on the first sustainability-linked facility.

sections.content:
The global market for sustainability-linked loans, green bonds, and transition finance instruments exceeded $4.5 trillion in outstanding volume in 2024. The pricing advantage for qualifying borrowers, typically 15 to 50 basis points on the coupon, represents a material cost-of-capital improvement for any enterprise with a significant debt program. For a company carrying $200 million in long-term debt, a 30-basis-point improvement is $600,000 per year in reduced interest expense. Compounded over a ten-year facility, it is a significant number.

Most enterprise CFOs are aware that these instruments exist. Most have been told by their bankers that their company "should qualify." Very few have actually accessed them. The gap between awareness and execution is not a financing problem. It's a data problem.
What Lenders Actually Require

Sustainability-linked financing instruments are priced against performance targets, specific, measurable commitments that the borrower makes at the time of issuance and is held to over the life of the facility. The most common targets involve Scope 1 and Scope 2 GHG emissions reductions, energy intensity improvements, and waste diversion rates. Some instruments also include Scope 3 targets, water efficiency metrics, and social performance indicators.

The critical requirement, the one that most companies fail to meet, is baseline auditability. Before a lender will price a sustainability-linked instrument, it needs to verify the borrower's starting point. Not a self-reported estimate. Not a consultant's projection. A quality-controlled, independently verifiable dataset that establishes where the company actually is today, so that progress against the target can be measured and confirmed.

This is where most companies fall short. Their sustainability data is fragmented across multiple systems, self-reported by facility managers, inconsistently defined across business units, and never subjected to the kind of quality control that financial data routinely receives. It's not audit-ready. And lenders know it.
The gap between awareness and execution is not a financing problem. It is a data problem. Most companies have the ambition. They do not have the baseline.

sections.content: The Baseline Problem in Practice

Consider a typical mid-market manufacturing company with 15 facilities across three provinces. Its sustainability team has been collecting energy and emissions data for three years. It has a disclosure report. It has ESG scores. It believes it has a baseline.

When Enduring Advantage's data team ingests this company's operational data, the pattern is consistent: approximately 30 to 40 percent of the data requires correction before it can be used as a financing baseline. Common issues include inconsistent metering boundaries between facilities, utility bill data that has not been normalised for production volume, refrigerant emissions that have been estimated rather than measured, and fleet data that conflates owned and leased vehicles. None of these issues are the result of negligence. They are the result of data being collected for disclosure purposes rather than financial purposes.

The difference matters enormously. A disclosure-grade baseline is sufficient to produce an ESG score. It's not sufficient to underpin a sustainability-linked loan covenant. Lenders require the latter. Most companies have only the former.
What an Audit-Ready Baseline Unlocks

The value of an audit-ready baseline extends well beyond financing. It's the foundation for every financial decision that touches sustainability: initiative prioritisation, M&V verification, regulatory compliance, and board-level reporting. Companies that invest in building a genuine baseline, quality-controlled, independently verifiable, and maintained over time, find that it pays for itself many times over.

The financing benefit alone is often sufficient to justify the investment. A company that qualifies for a sustainability-linked revolving credit facility at 25 basis points below its standard rate, on a $100 million facility, is saving $250,000 per year. The cost of building the baseline that unlocks that saving is typically a fraction of that figure. The payback period is measured in months, not years.

The companies that have figured this out are not waiting for their sustainability teams to get there organically. They are treating the baseline as a capital project, resourced, time-bound, and owned by the CFO's office. The return on that investment is not theoretical. It is on the income statement.

faq.question: What are Scope 3 emissions and why do they matter to CFOs?
faq.answer: Scope 3 emissions are the indirect emissions that occur across a company's value chain, in suppliers' factories, in customers' use of products, and in logistics networks. They represent more than 70 percent of a large enterprise's total carbon footprint on average. They matter to CFOs because regulatory mandates, investor pressure, and customer supply chain requirements are making them a financial risk management priority, not just a disclosure item.

faq.question: What regulations require Scope 3 disclosure?
faq.answer: The EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) requires Scope 3 disclosure for large EU-listed companies from 2026. The SEC climate rules in the United States and the ISSB S2 standard globally are also driving Scope 3 reporting requirements. Companies selling into automotive, consumer goods, financial services, and technology supply chains face customer-driven Scope 3 data requirements regardless of regulatory mandates.

faq.question: How should a CFO approach Scope 3 measurement?
faq.answer: Start with materiality, identify which of the 15 GHG Protocol Scope 3 categories are financially significant for your specific business. For most enterprises, three to five categories account for 80 percent of the Scope 3 footprint. Focus primary data collection and supplier engagement on those categories first, then build outward incrementally.

faq.question: What is the commercial risk of not managing Scope 3 emissions?
faq.answer: Large enterprise customers with their own net-zero commitments are increasingly requiring auditable Scope 3 data from suppliers as a condition of procurement. A supplier that cannot provide this data is progressively harder to do business with. This is already a present commercial reality in automotive, consumer goods, financial services, and technology supply chains.

sections.content:
Scope 3 emissions, the indirect emissions that occur across a company's value chain, upstream and downstream, represent, on average, more than 70 percent of a large enterprise's total carbon footprint. For some sectors, the figure is over 90 percent. For years, Scope 3 was treated as a voluntary disclosure item: something to estimate, report, and move on from. That era is ending.

The convergence of regulatory mandates (CSRD in Europe, SEC climate rules in the United States, ISSB S2 globally), investor due diligence requirements, and customer supply chain decarbonization programs has made Scope 3 a financial risk management priority. Companies that cannot measure, manage, and credibly disclose their Scope 3 emissions are increasingly finding themselves excluded from procurement programs, financing facilities, and investment portfolios. The cost of inaction is no longer theoretical.
Why Scope 3 Is Different

Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions are operationally owned. A company controls its own facilities, its own fleet, its own energy procurement. The data is available, the levers are identifiable, and the financial case for reduction is relatively straightforward. Scope 3 is different in every respect.

The emissions occur outside the company's operational boundary, in suppliers' factories, in customers' use of products, in the logistics networks that move goods between them. The company does not control these emissions directly. It influences them through procurement decisions, product design, supplier engagement, and customer incentive programs. The measurement challenge is correspondingly greater: Scope 3 data must be collected from hundreds or thousands of external parties, normalised across different reporting standards, and quality-controlled to a level that satisfies external scrutiny.

Most finance teams have not engaged seriously with this challenge. Scope 3 has been treated as a sustainability team problem, something to estimate using spend-based proxies and report in the annual disclosure. The estimates are often materially wrong. The proxies are often outdated. And the resulting disclosures are increasingly being challenged by investors, regulators, and customers who have their own data.

The Financial Risk Framing

The CFO's entry point into Scope 3 is not disclosure. It is risk. Specifically, it is the concentration risk embedded in the supply chain. A company that sources 60 percent of its key inputs from suppliers in a single geography, operating under a single regulatory regime, with a single energy mix, has a supply chain concentration risk that is directly correlated with carbon policy risk. When that regulatory regime tightens, as European carbon border adjustment mechanisms are already demonstrating, the cost of those inputs rises. The company that has mapped its Scope 3 exposure has the information it needs to diversify. The company that has not is flying blind.

The same logic applies to customer relationships. Large enterprise customers, particularly those with their own net-zero commitments, are increasingly requiring Scope 3 data from their suppliers as a condition of procurement. A company that cannot provide credible, auditable Scope 3 data is a supplier that is progressively harder to do business with. This isn't a future risk. It's a present commercial reality for companies selling into automotive, consumer goods, financial services, and technology supply chains.
What a Managed Scope 3 program Looks Like

A managed Scope 3 program is not a disclosure exercise. It's a supply chain risk management program with a carbon lens. It begins with materiality, identifying which Scope 3 categories are financially significant for the specific business, rather than attempting to measure all fifteen GHG Protocol categories with equal rigour. For most enterprises, three to five categories account for 80 percent of the Scope 3 footprint. Those are the ones that warrant investment in primary data collection and supplier engagement.

It then moves to supplier engagement, not the kind of engagement that produces a questionnaire response, but the kind that produces actual emissions data from actual suppliers. This requires a combination of data infrastructure, supplier incentive design, and procurement policy alignment. It's not a sustainability team project. It's a procurement and finance project with sustainability expertise applied to it.

The companies that have built this capability are finding that it delivers financial returns well beyond the compliance benefit. Better supplier data enables better procurement decisions. Supplier decarbonization programs reduce input cost volatility. And the credible Scope 3 disclosures that result unlock financing instruments and customer relationships that were not previously accessible. Scope 3 is not a burden. Managed correctly, it is a competitive advantage.

It moves the environmental agenda from the sustainability team to the CFO's office, applying the same capital allocation logic as any other investment category.

faq.question: What is the difference between ESG and Profitable Environmental Performance?
faq.answer: ESG is a broad framework covering environmental, social, and governance factors. Profitable Environmental Performance narrows the focus to the three environmental pillars with direct, measurable financial impact. Social and governance issues are separated out and addressed through different frameworks. The result is an environmental agenda that can be evaluated using financial return metrics rather than ESG scores.

faq.answer: A meta-analysis of over 2,000 empirical studies found that 63 percent showed a positive correlation between environmental performance and corporate financial performance, while only 8 percent showed a negative correlation. McKinsey research indicates that efficiency programs in energy and waste can affect operating profits by up to 60 percent.

faq.answer: Energy efficiency projects in buildings typically pay back in three to seven years. Waste reduction programs often pay back in under two years. Water efficiency investments in water-stressed regions can pay back in under a year. These are operational improvement investments with well-understood risk profiles, not long-dated uncertain bets.

sections.content:
The framework historically known as ESG is undergoing a fundamental restructuring. For a decade, the acronym served as a useful shorthand for a broad set of corporate responsibilities, environmental stewardship, social accountability, governance quality. It gave investors a common vocabulary and gave companies a reporting structure. It also, in the view of a growing number of CFOs and capital allocators, became too broad to be useful.

The shift that is now underway is not a retreat from environmental ambition. It's a sharpening of focus. The market is converging on what Enduring Advantage has long called Profitable Environmental Performance: a discipline that concentrates exclusively on the three environmental pillars that have demonstrable, measurable impact on enterprise value, climate change and decarbonization, biodiversity loss and natural capital, and pollution and the circular economy. Social and governance issues, while important, are being separated out and addressed through different frameworks and different teams.

For CFOs, this shift is significant. It means that the environmental portion of the sustainability agenda can now be evaluated using the same capital allocation logic as any other investment category. It means that the question is no longer “what is our ESG score?” but “what is the financial return on each environmental initiative, and how does it compare to the alternatives?”
The Three Pillars and Their Financial Mechanisms

The first pillar, climate change and decarbonization, is the most developed and the most directly connected to operating costs. For energy-intensive businesses, decarbonization is not a compliance exercise; it is an energy cost reduction program. Building operations alone account for 30 percent of global final energy consumption and 26 percent of global energy-related emissions. For any company with a significant real estate or manufacturing footprint, this is where the largest near-term financial returns are concentrated.

The second pillar, biodiversity loss and natural capital, is less familiar to most finance teams but increasingly material. Companies that depend on agricultural supply chains, water resources, or land use face growing exposure to natural capital constraints that translate directly into input cost volatility and supply chain disruption. The financial case for natural capital investment is not philanthropic; it is about securing the resource base that the business depends on.

The third pillar, pollution and the circular economy, is the most straightforward from a cost reduction perspective. Waste is a cost. Water is a cost. Raw materials are a cost. A circular economy model that minimises waste and maximises material reuse reduces all three. sections.content: The Evidence Base for ROI

The debate over whether environmental performance yields a financial return has been settled by the data. A meta-analysis of over 2,000 empirical studies by Friede, Busch, and Bassen found that 63 percent showed a positive correlation between environmental performance and corporate financial performance, while only 8 percent showed a negative correlation. McKinsey research indicates that efficiency programs in energy and waste can affect operating profits by up to 60 percent.

These can be material effects alongside major operational improvement programs in procurement, logistics, and manufacturing. The difference is that environmental performance initiatives have historically been managed by sustainability teams with limited capital allocation authority, evaluated against compliance benchmarks rather than financial return thresholds, and reported in sustainability reports rather than earnings calls.

The shift to Profitable Environmental Performance changes that. It moves the environmental agenda from the sustainability team to the CFO's office. It applies the same investment discipline, baseline measurement, ROI modelling, capital allocation, performance tracking, that the CFO applies to every other category of operational investment. And it produces results that are reported in the same financial terms as every other investment: cost reduction, margin improvement, risk-adjusted return on capital.

Environmental performance initiatives have historically been managed by sustainability teams with limited capital allocation authority. The shift to Profitable Environmental Performance moves the agenda to the CFO's office, where the returns are.
What This Means for Capital Allocation

For a CFO making capital allocation decisions in 2026, the practical implication of this shift is straightforward. Environmental performance initiatives should be evaluated on the same basis as any other investment: what is the expected return, what is the payback period, what is the risk-adjusted NPV, and how does it compare to the alternatives?

Research demonstrates that many sustainability-linked investments have shorter and more reliable payback periods than traditional growth initiatives. Energy efficiency projects in buildings typically pay back in three to seven years. Waste reduction programs often pay back in under two years. Water efficiency investments in water-stressed regions can pay back in under a year. These are not long-dated, uncertain bets. They are operational improvement investments with well-understood risk profiles.

The companies that are capturing these returns are not doing so by accident. They are doing so by treating environmental performance as a capital allocation discipline: measuring the baseline rigorously, modelling the returns conservatively, allocating capital to the highest-return initiatives first, and tracking performance against the financial targets they set at the outset. This is the discipline that Enduring Advantage brings to every client engagement, and it is the discipline that separates profitable environmental performance from sustainability theatre.

sections.content:
There's a phrase that circulates in sustainability advisory circles that captures the current moment precisely: the regulatory ratchet. A ratchet moves in one direction only. Once it advances, it does not retreat. The regulatory landscape for environmental disclosure has become a ratchet. The direction of travel is toward more disclosure, more rigour, more auditability, and more consequence for non-compliance. The pace of advance varies by jurisdiction and by political cycle, but the direction does not.

The evidence for this is not theoretical. The International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) has established a global baseline for climate-related financial disclosure that is now being adopted by regulators across more than 20 jurisdictions. The European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) under the CSRD have created the most comprehensive mandatory environmental reporting regime in history, covering over 50,000 companies operating in or selling into the European market. The TCFD framework, once voluntary, has been incorporated into mandatory reporting requirements in the UK, New Zealand, Switzerland, and a growing list of other countries.

The companies that are treating these frameworks as a compliance burden are making a strategic error. The companies that are treating them as a competitive weapon are building capabilities that will be very difficult for slower-moving peers to replicate.
Non-Compliance Is Now a Financial Risk

The consequences of non-compliance have moved well beyond reputational damage. Regulators worldwide are actively enforcing disclosure rules. Companies that fail to provide accurate, auditable environmental data face fines, restricted access to capital markets, and exclusion from major supply chains.

The supply chain exclusion risk is particularly significant for mid-market companies. Large multinationals are under pressure from their own regulators and investors to clean up their Scope 3 emissions, which means the emissions in their supply chains. A supplier that cannot provide auditable environmental data is a liability. In a competitive procurement environment, the supplier with the better data wins the contract. This dynamic is already playing out in automotive, consumer goods, and technology supply chains, and it is spreading rapidly to other sectors.

The capital markets dimension is equally significant. Green bonds and sustainability-linked loans now represent a substantial and growing share of corporate debt issuance. The interest rate advantage on sustainability-linked instruments is real and growing. Companies with strong, auditable environmental performance data can access this capital at a lower cost than companies without it. The cost of capital differential is not large enough to be transformative on its own, but it is large enough to be material in a capital allocation decision, and it compounds over time.
A supplier that cannot provide auditable environmental data is a liability. In a competitive procurement environment, the supplier with the better data wins the contract.
The Early Mover Advantage

The companies that invested early in environmental data infrastructure are now reaping a compounding advantage. Their data is cleaner, their baselines are more reliable, their reporting is faster and cheaper, and their ability to model the financial impact of environmental initiatives is more sophisticated. This capability gap between early movers and late movers is widening, not narrowing, because the early movers are continuing to invest while the late movers are still building the foundations.

The 2026 market pulse confirms this pattern. Despite some regulatory rollbacks, most notably the EU Omnibus Directive, which delayed certain CSRD requirements for smaller companies, the vast majority of large companies are continuing to invest in sustainability reporting infrastructure. They are doing so not because they are required to today, but because they recognise that market and investor demands require it regardless of specific mandates. The regulatory ratchet may pause, but it does not reverse.

For CFOs who have not yet made a serious investment in environmental data infrastructure, the question is not whether to invest, but how to invest efficiently. The answer is to start with the data that is most material to your specific business, the emissions, the water, the waste, the supply chain exposures that have the largest financial impact, and build outward from there. The companies that try to build comprehensive environmental data systems from scratch, covering everything at once, tend to spend a great deal of money and produce data of limited quality. The companies that start with materiality and build incrementally tend to produce better data at lower cost.

sections.content: The Multi-Framework Challenge

One of the most significant practical challenges facing finance teams in 2026 is the multi-framework environment. ISSB, ESRS, TCFD, GRI, CDP, SASB, each framework has different scope, different materiality definitions, different disclosure requirements, and different assurance standards. A company operating across multiple jurisdictions may be subject to several of these frameworks simultaneously, with overlapping but non-identical requirements.

The companies that are managing this complexity most effectively are those that have built a single, integrated environmental data platform that can generate outputs for multiple frameworks from a common data set. This isn't a trivial investment, but it is significantly cheaper than maintaining separate data collection and reporting processes for each framework. It also produces better data quality, because the discipline of reconciling outputs across frameworks forces a rigour in the underlying data that single-framework reporting does not require.

The strategic recommendation is to treat the multi-framework environment not as a compliance burden but as a data infrastructure investment. The companies that build this infrastructure now will be able to respond to new regulatory requirements faster and at lower cost than their competitors. They will also have better data for internal decision-making, which is, ultimately, the more valuable output.

faq.question: What is natural capital and why is it a financial risk?
faq.answer: Natural capital refers to the ecosystems, species, water systems, and biological processes that underpin economic activity. The World Economic Forum estimates that more than half of global GDP, approximately USD 44 trillion, is moderately or highly dependent on nature. When these natural systems degrade, companies face physical risk (operational disruption), transition risk (regulatory and market shifts), and liability risk (legal exposure for contributing to biodiversity loss).

faq.question: Why is natural capital risk systematically underestimated by finance teams?
faq.answer: Three structural reasons: natural capital does not appear on the balance sheet (it is treated as a free input by conventional accounting); the time horizon of natural capital depletion is longer than most corporate planning cycles; and the measurement frameworks for nature risk are less mature than those for climate, the TNFD only published its final recommendations in 2023.

faq.question: Which industries face the greatest natural capital risk?
faq.answer: Agriculture, food and beverage, consumer goods, real estate, and manufacturing face the highest exposure. For these sectors, natural capital dependencies are embedded in the supply chain, the production process, and the physical assets the business depends on. Agricultural commodity supply chains are particularly exposed to deforestation, soil degradation, water depletion, and pollinator decline.

faq.question: What is the TNFD and what does it require?
faq.answer: The Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD) published its final recommendations in 2023, creating a disclosure framework for nature-related financial risks and opportunities. Modelled on the TCFD for climate, it asks companies to assess their dependencies and impacts on nature, identify material risks and opportunities, and disclose them in financial filings. Regulatory adoption is accelerating across multiple jurisdictions.

sections.content:
There's a category of risk on most corporate balance sheets that is not measured, not disclosed, and not managed. It does not appear in the standard risk register. It's not covered by most insurance policies. It's not captured by any of the major financial reporting frameworks, though that is beginning to change. It's the risk that arises from the depletion of natural capital, the ecosystems, species, water systems, and biological processes that underpin a significant portion of global economic activity.

The World Economic Forum estimates that more than half of global GDP, approximately USD 44 trillion of economic value generation, is moderately or highly dependent on nature and its services. For companies in agriculture, food and beverage, consumer goods, real estate, and manufacturing, the dependency is not abstract. It is embedded in the supply chain, the production process, and the physical assets that the business depends on.

The financial risks that arise from natural capital depletion fall into three categories that finance teams are familiar with from other risk domains: physical risk (the direct impact of ecosystem degradation on operations and assets), transition risk (the regulatory and market shifts that will occur as natural capital constraints become more acute), and liability risk (the legal and reputational exposure that arises from contributing to biodiversity loss).
Why This Risk Is Systematically Underestimated

Natural capital risk is systematically underestimated for a set of reasons that are structural rather than accidental. First, natural capital does not appear on the balance sheet. Unlike financial capital, physical capital, and even human capital (in the form of workforce costs), natural capital is treated as a free input by conventional accounting. The cost of water is the cost of extraction and treatment, not the cost of the aquifer. The cost of pollination is zero, because pollinators are not purchased. The cost of flood protection is the cost of insurance, not the cost of the wetlands that provide it.

Second, the time horizon of natural capital depletion is longer than most corporate planning cycles. The degradation of an aquifer, the collapse of a pollinator population, or the erosion of a coastal wetland typically occurs over decades, not quarters. This makes it easy to defer the risk assessment to the next planning cycle, and the one after that, until the risk materialises as an acute operational disruption.

Third, the measurement frameworks for natural capital are less mature than those for climate. The TCFD framework for climate risk has been in development since 2015 and is now well-established. The equivalent framework for nature, the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD), only published its final recommendations in 2023. The data infrastructure for nature risk measurement is still being built.

More than half of global GDP is moderately or highly dependent on nature and its services. For companies in agriculture, food and beverage, and manufacturing, this dependency is not abstract, it is embedded in the supply chain.

sections.content: The Supply Chain Dimension

For most companies, the most significant natural capital risk is not in their own operations but in their supply chains. Agricultural commodity supply chains are particularly exposed. Deforestation, soil degradation, water depletion, and pollinator decline are all affecting the productivity and reliability of agricultural supply chains in ways that translate directly into input cost volatility and supply security risk.

The companies that are managing this risk most effectively are those that have mapped their supply chain dependencies on natural capital with the same rigour that they apply to financial and operational risk. This means identifying which inputs are most exposed to natural capital constraints, which geographies are most at risk, and which suppliers are most dependent on the natural systems that are under greatest pressure.

This isn't a simple exercise. Natural capital dependencies are often indirect and multi-layered. A food manufacturer may not directly depend on a specific forest, but its key ingredient suppliers may depend on the water systems that the forest regulates. Mapping these dependencies requires data that most supply chain teams do not currently collect, and analytical frameworks that most risk teams have not yet developed.

sections.content: The Opportunity Side of the Ledger

Natural capital is not only a risk category. It's also an opportunity category. Companies that invest in nature-based solutions, reforestation, wetland restoration, regenerative agriculture, sustainable water management, are finding that these investments deliver financial returns through multiple mechanisms: supply chain resilience, input cost reduction, regulatory compliance, and access to the growing market for high-quality nature credits.

Microsoft's April 2026 agreement to purchase 626,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide removal from a BECCS project in Saskatchewan, a 15-year, landmark deal structured around bioenergy with carbon capture and storage, illustrates how nature-based and nature-adjacent solutions are becoming major capital markets instruments. The deal provides Microsoft with the durable carbon removal it needs to meet its climate targets, while providing the project developers with the long-term revenue certainty required to finance the infrastructure. It's a template for how environmental goals can drive major capital investments and create new markets.

For CFOs, the practical implication is to treat natural capital as a balance sheet item that needs to be measured, managed, and reported, not because regulators currently require it in most jurisdictions, but because the financial risks and opportunities it represents are material and growing. The companies that build this capability now will be better positioned to manage the risks, capture the opportunities, and meet the disclosure requirements that are coming. The companies that wait will be building under pressure, at higher cost, with less time to develop the data quality that credible disclosure requires.

There's a question every CFO should ask before engaging a sustainability advisor: how does this firm make money? The answer helps the CFO understand how recommendations and delivery costs are structured.

The sustainability advisory market is commercially varied. Firms may earn revenue from equipment installation, product sales, referral fees from vendors, or extended engagement retainers. Each structure should be clear before capital is committed. An advisor who earns a commission on a heat pump installation has a reason to recommend that installation. An advisor who takes referral fees from vendors has a financial relationship the client should know about.

This is not a criticism of individual practitioners. It is a structural question. When commercial incentives and the client’s interests point in different directions, the client needs disclosure and an evidence-led process.
How the Conflict Manifests in Practice

Commercial structure can shape advice in three ways.

The first is solution bias. An advisor who sells or installs a particular category of solution, such as solar, LED lighting, HVAC controls, or EV fleet, may overweight that category in its recommendations. The client's opportunity set is not organized around the advisor's product catalogue. The highest-return move could be in procurement, waste, water, or supply chain.

The second is baseline quality. Savings should be measured against a clear, traceable baseline. Where an early figure begins as a vendor estimate, it should be labelled as an estimate and later replaced with verified results.

The third is delivery transparency. Clients should know what work is included, what specialist costs are passed through, and how the recommendation is insulated from equipment sales and referral fees.
A commercial structure is not a judgment on individual practitioners. It is information a client should understand before acting on the advice.

Genuine independence starts with a structure the client can see. Enduring Advantage does not earn installation revenue, sell products, or take referral fees. Coach and specialist time is passed through at cost, with no markup. The advisory fee is a retainer plus a share of verified results.

The Questions Every CFO Should Ask

Before engaging any sustainability advisor, a CFO should ask four questions.

First: does the firm earn revenue from installation or equipment sales? Second: does it take referral fees or commissions from vendors? Third: what delivery costs are passed through, and on what terms? Fourth: who verifies the baseline and the result?

These are not adversarial questions. They help the client understand the commercial structure, compare proposals, and make a decision with clear evidence.

The data gap between reporting and returns

Most organizations are stuck in a reporting cycle. They gather data once a year to satisfy a regulatory requirement or produce a glossy PDF. That's a cost centre. To turn environmental performance into a profit engine, the data must be granular enough to drive daily procurement and production decisions.

We see companies spending millions on carbon offsets, a pure expense, while missing internal rate of return (IRR) opportunities in their own supply chains. If you can't see the specific energy intensity of a single production line in real-time, you can't manage the margin on the product coming off that line. Independent, vendor-agnostic analysis is the only way to find these gaps without being sold a pre-packaged software solution that only tracks what happened in the past.
Shifting from compliance to margin protection

Compliance is a baseline, but the real financial win is margin protection. As carbon taxes and resource scarcity become more prevalent in 2026, the businesses that have integrated environmental units into their financial modeling will be the ones that maintain stable pricing.

By treating environmental inputs as a high-ROI operational category, CFOs can justify capital expenditures that pay for themselves in reduced waste and lower energy intensity. This isn't about being green; it's about being lean in a resource-constrained market.
