Innovation Vista put it most directly: "The difference between a strategy that gets executed and one that gathers dust is almost always the presence of an accountable leader on the other side of the deliverable."

Most CFOs have experienced this. A credible firm arrives, conducts a thorough assessment, produces an immaculate strategy document, presents it to the board, and then leaves. Twelve months later, the document is still on the shelf. The initiatives it recommended have not been funded, staffed, or started. The targets the company announced publicly are quietly receding.

This isn't a strategy problem. The strategy was probably sound. It is an accountability problem. And it is the most expensive problem in sustainability today.
Why the Standard Model Produces Shelf-Ware

The Big-4 and strategy consulting model is built around diagnosis and recommendation. The partner who leads the engagement is paid to produce a high-quality plan. They are not paid, and their economics do not support, staying on site to manage the procurement of a heat-recovery system in a manufacturing facility in Mississauga or the renegotiation of a power purchase agreement for a distribution centre in the Netherlands.

This isn't a criticism. It's a structural reality. The model that makes strategy consulting profitable is incompatible with the model that makes execution happen. The CFO who commissions a six-figure strategy engagement and expects execution to follow is misunderstanding what they bought.

The result is predictable: 47% of finance leaders express doubt that their organization will actually hit the sustainability commitments it has already made publicly. That is not a confidence problem. It's a rational assessment of a system with no accountable owner at the execution stage.

sections.content: The Three Conditions for Execution

In our experience, sustainability initiatives get executed when three conditions are present simultaneously. Remove any one of them and the initiative stalls.

**A named accountable owner.** Not a committee. Not a shared responsibility. A specific person, internal or external, who is accountable for the outcome and whose engagement does not end when the strategy document is delivered. This person must have the authority to convene the relevant functions, the subject-matter expertise to evaluate options, and the mandate to make decisions without re-escalating every choice to the CFO.

**A payback number attached to each initiative.** Sustainability initiatives compete for capital against every other investment the organization can make. Without a credible, source-graded financial return estimate attached to each initiative, they will lose that competition every time. The CFO's own bar, documented in multiple surveys, is three years or less. Any initiative that cannot demonstrate a three-year financial return in the current capital environment will not get funded, regardless of its environmental merit.

**A vendor-neutral selection process.** The single fastest way to destroy execution momentum is to have the advisory firm that recommended an initiative also profit from its implementation. When the advisor has a financial relationship with the vendor they are recommending, the CFO's defensibility evaporates. The board will ask the question. The auditor will ask the question. The answer must be clean.

The CFO who commissions a six-figure strategy engagement and expects execution to follow is misunderstanding what they bought. Strategy and execution are different products. Most firms only sell one of them.
What Board-Defensible Execution Looks Like

A board-defensible sustainability program has a specific structure. It begins with a verified baseline, not a self-reported estimate, but an auditable measurement of current operational performance across energy, water, waste, and material inputs. Without this, every projected saving is a guess, and the board will treat it as one.

From the verified baseline, each candidate initiative is scored against four criteria: projected savings in dollars, projected GHG reduction, financial return, and financing eligibility. The initiatives are ranked. The highest-ranking initiative, the one with the greatest material impact relative to its cost and complexity, is selected first. It is executed. The results are measured against the baseline. Then the process repeats.

This isn't a novel methodology. It's the application of standard capital allocation discipline to sustainability. The reason it is rare is not that it is difficult. It is that most advisory models are not designed to stay through execution. They are designed to leave after the ranking.

Enduring Advantage is designed around the opposite principle. The coach and the subject-matter experts remain engaged through execution, through measurement, and through the next iteration. The accountability does not end when the deck is delivered. It ends when the result is on the income statement.

sections.content: The Four Data Problems CFOs Actually Face

EY's research identifies the specific failure modes with precision: varying data formats (39%), inconsistencies between sources (35%), incomplete records (34%), and unclear definitions (33%). These are not abstract data-governance concerns. They are the specific reasons a CFO cannot answer a pointed question from the audit committee without hedging.

**Varying formats** mean that energy consumption data from a facility in Calgary arrives in gigajoules, from a facility in London in kilowatt-hours, and from a facility in Singapore in a spreadsheet with no units labelled. Aggregating these into a single portfolio number requires assumptions. Assumptions are not defensible.

**Inconsistencies** mean that the same metric, say, Scope 2 electricity emissions, is calculated using market-based accounting in one region and location-based accounting in another. The number looks like a single figure. It's not.

**Incomplete records** mean that a facility acquired two years ago has no historical baseline. The company's reported progress since the acquisition is measured against a starting point that does not exist.

**Unclear definitions** mean that "waste diverted from landfill" includes composting in one facility and incineration-with-energy-recovery in another. Both are reported as the same metric. They are not the same thing.
Once finance leaders drill into the data and see how much needs to be done, their conservative tendency kicks in, with a healthy skepticism about the organization's ability to hit those commitments.
What a Verified Baseline Actually Requires

A verified baseline is not a self-reported estimate. It is an auditable measurement of actual operational performance, energy consumption by meter, water use by facility, waste output by stream, with a clear methodology, a named data source, and a documented quality-control process.

Building one requires four things that most organizations do not currently have in place:

**Meter-level data collection.** Not utility bill aggregates. Not engineering estimates. Actual consumption data from the point of use, collected at a frequency that allows anomaly detection.

**A single methodology applied consistently.** The same calculation approach, the same emission factors, the same boundary definitions, applied to every facility in the portfolio.

**A quality-control layer.** A process that flags data that falls outside expected ranges, identifies missing records, and requires resolution before the data is included in the baseline.

**An audit trail.** Every number in the baseline traceable back to a primary source, a meter reading, a utility invoice, a waste manifest, with a documented chain of custody.
The Payback on Getting the Data Right

There's a direct financial return on data quality investment that most organizations miss entirely. When the baseline is verified and the data is clean, the organization can identify with precision where the largest operational inefficiencies are. Not at the portfolio level, at the facility level, at the process level, at the equipment level.

This precision is what converts a sustainability program from a cost centre into a profit driver. The IEA estimates that energy efficiency alone can deliver more than a third of all carbon reductions to 2030, and that it is "most often cost-effective." BCG and CO2 AI research documents that 82% of companies that pursued decarbonization captured measurable economic benefit, with leaders netting an average of $221 million per company.

Those results are not available to organizations operating on unverified data. You cannot optimize what you cannot measure. And you cannot defend what you cannot trace.

The CFO who invests in a verified baseline is not spending money on compliance infrastructure. They are building the foundation for every profitable sustainability initiative that follows, and the defensibility that makes every board conversation about sustainability a conversation about value creation, not exposure.

sections.content: The Compliance-First Trap

The compliance-first approach to sustainability has a structural flaw that the current regulatory environment has made impossible to ignore: it frames every sustainability investment as a cost, and it ties the business case for that cost to a specific regulatory requirement.

When the requirement changes, and it will change, as it has just changed dramatically in both the EU and the US, the business case evaporates. The CFO who approved a $2 million investment in CSRD compliance infrastructure in 2024 is now explaining to the board why that investment was necessary. The CFO who approved a $2 million investment in energy efficiency in 2024 is showing the board the $600,000 in annual savings it generated.

The compliance-first frame also creates a specific political vulnerability: it associates the company's sustainability program with regulatory obligation rather than business performance. In the current environment, where 87% of US companies are maintaining or increasing sustainability investment but doing it quietly, and only 25% of S&P 500 firms still use "ESG" in their report titles, the compliance-first frame is the wrong frame.

The profitable moves in sustainability are robust to regulatory whiplash. A company that reduces its energy consumption by 30% saves money whether or not there is a disclosure requirement. The financial case does not depend on the regulatory case.
What Regulatory Resilience Actually Means

Regulatory resilience is not about ignoring regulation. It is about building a sustainability program whose business case does not depend on any specific regulatory requirement.

The test is simple: if the relevant regulation were rescinded tomorrow, would this initiative still deliver a positive return? If the answer is yes, the initiative is regulatory-resilient. If the answer is no, if the only reason to do it is to satisfy a reporting requirement, then it is regulatory-fragile.

Energy efficiency passes the test. Waste reduction passes the test. Supply chain optimization passes the test. Water use reduction passes the test. These initiatives deliver operational savings that flow directly to the income statement, regardless of what the regulator does.

Carbon offset purchases, in most cases, do not pass the test. Compliance reporting infrastructure, in most cases, does not pass the test.
The Incentive Window That Is Actually Closing

There is one genuine urgency argument in the current environment that is not about compliance. The US One Big Beautiful Budget Act (OBBBA), signed in July 2025, phases out the IRA's clean-electricity credits. Construction must begin by July 4, 2026 or be in service by December 31, 2027 to qualify.

For multi-site companies with energy-intensive operations, this is a real and closing window. The economics of certain renewable energy and efficiency investments are materially better before the credit phases out than after. This isn't a compliance argument. It's a capital allocation argument: the same investment delivers a better return if made now than if made in 2028.

This is the kind of regulatory context that belongs in a sustainability program, not as a compliance driver, but as a capital allocation input. The question is not "what do we have to do before the deadline?" It is "what is the most profitable thing we can do before this incentive closes, and how do we fund it?"

The answer to that question is different for every company, at every location. It requires a verified baseline, a systematic evaluation of options, and a vendor-neutral selection process. It is available from an advisor who sits on the buyer's side of the table and whose only interest is in the quality of the outcome.

faq.question: Why is nature loss a financial risk for companies?
faq.answer: More than half of global GDP is moderately or highly dependent on nature and the services it provides, including water regulation, soil fertility, pollination, and climate stability. Companies with supply chains that depend on these services face input cost volatility, procurement disruption, and stranded asset risk as ecosystems degrade. These are balance sheet exposures, not environmental abstractions.

faq.question: How is biodiversity risk different from carbon risk?
faq.answer: Carbon risk is largely global and fungible: a tonne of CO2 emitted in one location has the same atmospheric effect as a tonne emitted elsewhere. Biodiversity risk is location-specific. The financial exposure depends on where in the world a company sources inputs, which ecosystems those supply chains depend on, and how degraded those ecosystems are. This makes it harder to measure and harder to aggregate, which is exactly why most companies have not yet priced it.

faq.answer: The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, agreed in 2022, commits countries to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030, restore degraded ecosystems, and mobilise at least $200 billion per year from public and private sources for nature-positive investment. Corporate disclosure requirements are expected to follow as governments translate these commitments into national legislation.

faq.answer: The first step is a supply chain dependency assessment: mapping which inputs, locations, and processes are exposed to nature-related risks. The third is building the data baseline that will be required for disclosure and for accessing nature-linked financing instruments. sections.content:
On August 4, 2025, Reuters reported that the United Nations biodiversity chief, Astrid Schomaker, told a press briefing that companies and financial institutions are not moving fast enough to address nature loss. Her specific language is worth noting: companies are aware that there is a risk, but they are not yet acting on it.

For a CFO, that sentence should land differently than it does for a sustainability manager. Awareness without action is not a neutral position. It's a documented liability. When a material risk is identified and not addressed, the question that follows in a boardroom, or a courtroom, is not whether the company knew. It is what the company did once it knew.

The paradox is that biodiversity and nature risk has been amongst the top risks for the past five or six years. So in a way they are aware that there is a risk, but companies are not yet acting on it.

sections.content: What the Numbers Actually Say

The World Economic Forum has listed biodiversity loss among its top global risks every year since 2020. A 2023 UN study found that more than $7 trillion was invested in environmentally harmful activities in a single year, most of it by the private sector. Research released last week found that tropical forests alone hold up to $1.2 trillion in undiscovered pharmaceutical value from flowering plants.

These are not advocacy statistics. They are capital allocation signals. The $7 trillion figure means that a substantial portion of corporate investment is actively creating the conditions for future supply chain disruption, regulatory liability, and asset impairment. The $1.2 trillion figure means that the financial value embedded in functioning ecosystems is orders of magnitude larger than most corporate balance sheets acknowledge.

The gap between what nature is worth and what companies are paying to protect it is not a moral failing. It's a pricing failure. And pricing failures, in the long run, correct themselves, usually at the expense of whoever was slowest to act.

sections.content: Why Companies Are Not Acting: The Real Reasons

Schomaker identified two structural barriers: companies have been slow to assess biodiversity risks, and governments have yet to require greater disclosure. Both are true, but they describe the symptom rather than the cause.

The deeper problem is that biodiversity risk is location-specific and hard to measure in a way that carbon risk is not. A company can calculate its Scope 1 and 2 emissions with a reasonable degree of confidence using energy bills and emissions factors. Biodiversity risk requires knowing which specific ecosystems your supply chain depends on, what the degradation trajectory of those ecosystems looks like, and how that trajectory intersects with your procurement costs, your input availability, and your regulatory exposure in each jurisdiction.

That is a harder analytical problem. It requires data that most companies do not have, a methodology that most advisory firms do not offer, and a willingness to look at the supply chain with a level of granularity that most sustainability programs have not yet reached.

The result is exactly what Schomaker described: awareness without action. Companies know the risk is real. They do not know where to start.
The Decision Paralysis Problem, Applied to Nature

The nature and biodiversity space has the same structural problem as the broader sustainability market: too many options, too little clarity about which ones actually move the needle.

There are now hundreds of nature-positive investment frameworks, certification schemes, offset markets, supply chain traceability tools, and ecosystem service valuation methodologies competing for corporate attention. The Cali Fund, launched at COP16 in 2024, is attempting to channel money from sectors that profit from genetic resources into conservation, but key questions about contribution structures, benefit-sharing, and eligibility remain unresolved.

For a CFO trying to make a defensible capital allocation decision, this landscape is not an opportunity. It's a source of decision paralysis. The question is not whether to engage with nature risk. The question is which engagement delivers the strongest financial return for your specific organization, at your specific locations, with your specific supply chain dependencies.

That question requires a systematic evaluation process, not a framework selection exercise.
Redirecting private capital towards nature-positive investments remains the biggest challenge.

The next round of CBD talks takes place in Armenia in October 2025, with preparatory sessions already underway in Nairobi. COP17 will include a formal review of corporate progress against the Kunming-Montreal Framework. Disclosure requirements are expected to tighten as governments translate their 2022 commitments into national legislation.

For CFOs, the window between now and COP17 is not a compliance countdown. It's a preparation opportunity. Companies that arrive at the next disclosure cycle with a verified supply chain dependency assessment, a clear nature-investment decision, and a data baseline that supports both internal reporting and external financing will be in a materially different position than those that do not.

The practical starting point is not a biodiversity strategy. It's a supply chain audit: which inputs, at which locations, depend on which ecosystem services, and what is the financial exposure if those services degrade. That audit produces the data that makes every subsequent decision, investment, disclosure, and financing conversation, more defensible.

The companies that will be best positioned after COP17 are not the ones with the most ambitious nature commitments. They are the ones that turned their awareness into a defensible first action before the disclosure requirements made it compulsory.

sections.content:
There's a conversation coming in your client relationships, and the question is whether you are the one who starts it or the one who gets asked to catch up.

A commentary published in One Earth in 2026 by Ripple, Wolf, Rockstrom, and colleagues argues that several major climate systems, including the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, Arctic permafrost, and the Amazon rainforest, may be closer to destabilisation than previously thought. These are not incremental risks. They are threshold risks: systems that, once pushed past a certain point, can begin changing in self-reinforcing ways that are difficult or impossible to reverse.

For a financial advisor or accountant, the immediate question is not whether the science is right. It is whether your clients' financial plans, risk assessments, and capital allocation decisions account for the possibility that the world changes faster and less predictably than the models they were built on assume.
The real exposure is not just the climate system itself, but the way environmental stress interacts with economic and operational systems.
What the Polycrisis Actually Means for Client Portfolios

The word polycrisis has moved from academic papers into mainstream risk frameworks. The environmental polycrisis has three connected parts: climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution. Each can make the others harder to manage.

For clients, this matters in practical ways. A manufacturing client with supply chain concentration in a water-stressed region can face input scarcity, price volatility, logistics disruption, and insurance gaps at the same time. A property client in a coastal or flood-prone area can face insurance withdrawal, financing constraints, and asset impairment before physical damage occurs.

The polycrisis lens does not replace standard risk categories. It connects them. For advisors, that connection is where the advice gap lives.
Why the conditions are changing faster than expected

We've been hearing the warnings for about 60 years. There's no more room to wait. Things are happening faster and in ways nobody expects. Nobody in France thought unexploded bombs would detonate under wildfires in the middle of their towns. Wildfires, deforestation, flooding, and drought are interrelated. Declining carbon sinks used to absorb roughly half of human emissions. They now absorb much less.

Corporations get dragged into global problems. They're already involved and will only get more involved. By the time it is obvious, it is too late. The proactive organizations will do dramatically better than those who wait. Supply chains are globally interconnected: fires in Europe or disruption in a strait raise costs and create shortages downstream. We can have a material impact if we do the right things, in the right order, at speed.

Supply Chain Exposure: Fires, floods, and port disruptions in one region create cost spikes and shortages downstream. Understanding your supply chain vulnerabilities is the first step to managing them.

Regulatory Momentum: Mandatory disclosure frameworks are expanding. Companies that have already built a verified baseline and a defensible first action are positioned to respond, not scramble.

Capital Access: Green financing, sustainability-linked loans, and ESG-screened investment are growing. The companies with auditable data and a credible program access better terms.
The Advice Gap That Is Opening Right Now

Most financial planning and accounting frameworks were built for a world of gradual, predictable change. Inflation moves within a range. Input costs rise steadily. Asset values follow long-run trends. The polycrisis introduces a different kind of risk: nonlinear change, where conditions appear stable until a threshold is crossed and then shift rapidly.

This creates a specific problem for advisors. If a client's five-year financial plan assumes gradual energy cost increases but their primary manufacturing region faces simultaneous water stress, grid instability, and supply chain disruption, the plan is not just optimistic. It is structurally incomplete. The advisor who helped build it carries some of that exposure.

The clients who are most exposed are often the ones who feel least urgency. They are profitable, operationally stable, and not yet facing regulatory pressure. But their supply chains, asset bases, and financing structures may carry concentrations that will become visible only when conditions change.

The conversation that opens this up is not a sustainability conversation. It's a risk conversation. It starts with questions your clients are already asking: what are our biggest cost exposures over the next three to five years, where are we most dependent on inputs or infrastructure that could become less reliable, and are our insurance and financing arrangements stress-tested for conditions that are more volatile than the last decade?
What Advisors Can Do Without Becoming Climate Experts

The good news is that financial advisors, accountants, and industry associations do not need to become climate scientists to serve clients well in this environment. The capability gap is not technical knowledge. It's the ability to connect environmental risk to financial outcomes in a way that is specific, quantified, and actionable.

There are four things advisors can do immediately.

First, add environmental stress scenarios to existing risk conversations. When reviewing a client's risk register or financial plan, ask whether the scenarios include simultaneous shocks rather than single-event disruptions. A client who can absorb a 15 percent energy cost increase may not be able to absorb a 15 percent energy cost increase at the same time as a 20 percent input cost increase and a logistics disruption.

Second, review supply chain and asset concentration through a resilience lens. Concentration risk is a concept every financial advisor understands. Applying it to geographic and ecosystem exposure is a natural extension of existing practice.

Third, ask whether insurance coverage and financing arrangements have been reviewed against a more volatile operating environment. Insurance markets are already repricing in exposed regions. Clients who have not reviewed their coverage recently may be carrying gaps they are not aware of.

Fourth, identify which clients have sustainability investment decisions pending and ensure those decisions are being made with the same rigour applied to capital allocation decisions generally. The question is not whether to invest in sustainability. It is which investments deliver the strongest financial return in the right order.
The firms that will be best positioned are the ones that treat climate and nature risk as a core financial planning issue rather than a peripheral sustainability issue.

heldForEditorialReview.subtitle: Property values collapse when a critical mass expects flooding. It does not have to happen first. Here is what that means for your balance sheet.

faq.question: What is strategic location planning in a sustainability context?
faq.answer: Strategic location planning is the process of assessing where to operate, invest, or expand based on long-term environmental risk factors including sea level rise, flood expectation, insurance availability, proximity to fresh water, and supply chain resilience. It is a risk management discipline, not an environmental one.

faq.question: Do I need to be in a coastal city to face flood risk?
faq.answer: No. Flood risk is driven by changing rainfall patterns, river systems, and urban drainage capacity, not just proximity to the ocean. Inland cities across Canada and the US have seen significant flood events in recent years. The relevant question is whether your properties sit in a catchment area that is changing.

faq.question: How does insurance withdrawal affect property values?
faq.answer: When major insurers exit a market or raise premiums to unaffordable levels, lenders become unwilling to underwrite mortgages on those properties. Without mortgage availability, the buyer pool shrinks, and values fall. This sequence has already played out in parts of Florida, California, and Louisiana.

faq.question: What is supply chain shortening and why does it matter?
faq.answer: Supply chain shortening is the deliberate strategy of reducing the geographic distance between your operations and your key suppliers. Shorter supply chains are less exposed to port disruptions, geopolitical events, and extreme weather in distant regions. They also reduce Scope 3 emissions and improve delivery reliability.

sections.content: The biggest location risks on your balance sheet are not the ones that have already happened. They are the ones that a growing number of people expect to happen. When expectation reaches a tipping point, property values move before the flood does. Insurance withdraws before the hurricane arrives. The financial consequence precedes the physical event by years.

This is the mechanism that makes strategic location planning a CFO-level conversation, not a facilities management one. It is not about whether your building will flood in 2040. It is about whether your lenders, insurers, and buyers will still be in the market for it in 2028.
The Expectation Mechanism

Property markets are forward-looking. When a critical mass of buyers, lenders, and insurers begins to price in a risk, values adjust regardless of whether the risk has materialised. We have already seen this sequence play out in coastal Florida, wildfire-exposed California, and hurricane-prone Louisiana. Insurers exit first. Premiums rise to unaffordable levels, or coverage becomes unavailable entirely. Without insurance, lenders will not underwrite mortgages. Without mortgage availability, the buyer pool shrinks to cash buyers only. Values fall.

The sequence is not hypothetical. State Farm and Allstate stopped writing new homeowner policies in California in 2023. In Florida, more than a dozen insurers have left the market since 2020. The properties affected have not necessarily flooded or burned. They are simply located where the expectation of those events has become widespread enough to change financial behaviour.
Property values collapse when a critical mass expects flooding. It does not have to happen first.
The Four Dimensions of Location Risk
Strategic location risk has four distinct dimensions, each with a different financial mechanism and a different time horizon.

Sea level rise and flood expectation risk is the most widely discussed but least well understood. The relevant metric is not the projected sea level in 2100. It is the point at which enough market participants begin pricing in that projection. In many coastal markets, that tipping point is closer than most CFOs assume.

Insurance availability is the canary in the coal mine. Insurers have access to the most sophisticated climate risk models in the world, and they price accordingly. When they exit a market, they are signalling something that the property market has not yet fully priced. Watch where the major carriers are withdrawing, and you have a leading indicator of where property values will follow.

Proximity to fresh drinking water and local food security are longer-horizon risks, but they are already influencing site selection decisions for data centres, manufacturing facilities, and agricultural operations. The regions with reliable access to fresh water and stable growing conditions will attract investment. The regions without them will face capital flight.

Supply chain geography is the most actionable dimension in the near term. The pandemic exposed the fragility of extended global supply chains. Extreme weather events, port disruptions, and geopolitical instability have reinforced that lesson repeatedly since. Shortening supply chains reduces exposure to all of these risks simultaneously, while also reducing Scope 3 emissions and improving delivery reliability.

sections.content: Staying Out of the Floodplain

The most effective strategic location decision is the one made before a property is acquired. Floodplain mapping has improved significantly in recent years, but most corporate real estate decisions still do not incorporate forward-looking climate risk assessments. The standard practice is to check current flood zone designations, which reflect historical data, not projected future conditions.

A forward-looking assessment incorporates sea level rise projections, changing precipitation patterns, urban heat island effects on local weather, and the upstream catchment conditions that determine how quickly a site floods when rainfall is heavy. It also incorporates the insurance market outlook for the specific geography, which is a more reliable signal than any single climate model.
The Supply Chain Shortening Opportunity

Supply chain shortening is unusual among sustainability initiatives because it addresses financial risk, environmental performance, and operational resilience simultaneously. A shorter supply chain is less exposed to disruption, generates fewer transport emissions, and is typically more responsive to demand changes. It is also easier to audit for ESG compliance, which matters increasingly for green financing eligibility.

The financial case for supply chain shortening has strengthened considerably since 2020. The cost of supply chain disruption is now better understood and better quantified. The availability of near-shore and domestic suppliers has improved as investment in regional manufacturing has increased. And the green financing instruments available to companies with credible supply chain sustainability programs have expanded significantly.
What This Means for the Sustainability Playing Field

Strategic location planning sits in the Risk Management column of the Sustainability Playing Field for a reason. It is not primarily an environmental initiative. It is a financial risk management discipline that happens to have significant environmental co-benefits. The companies that treat it as such will make better decisions than those who frame it as a sustainability project.

The Enduring Advantage methodology evaluates strategic location risk as part of the broader risk management assessment. It is one of 36 dimensions across the playing field, and like all of them, it is only recommended when the financial and environmental case is positive. For some organizations, the biggest opportunity on the playing field will be in operational efficiency or decarbonization. For others, it will be in understanding and managing the location risk embedded in their existing portfolio.

The point of starting from the widest possible field is precisely this: you cannot know in advance which dimension holds your biggest opportunity. The organizations that narrow the field before they start will miss it. The ones that begin with the whole field and let the data determine the answer are more likely to find it.
The biggest opportunity is rarely where you expect it. Start from the widest possible field and let the data determine the sector, the initiative, and the order.

heldForEditorialReview.title: TNFD: What Financial Advisors Need to Know Before Their Clients Ask
heldForEditorialReview.subtitle: The nature-risk disclosure framework your clients will face next
heldForEditorialReview.heroAlt: Forest canopy representing nature-related financial risk and biodiversity
heldForEditorialReview.excerpt: The Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures is moving from voluntary to mandatory in several jurisdictions. Here is what it means for the clients of financial advisors, accountants, and industry associations.
heldForEditorialReview.author: Campbell Ohrlis

sections.content: Your clients are about to receive a new set of disclosure requirements that most of them have never heard of. The Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures, known as TNFD, is the biodiversity and nature-risk equivalent of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. TCFD is now mandatory in the UK, Canada, New Zealand, and several other jurisdictions. TNFD is following the same path, and faster than most people expect.

The difference between TCFD and TNFD is that nature risk is harder to quantify, harder to locate, and harder to price than carbon risk. Carbon has a single unit of measurement and a growing number of market prices. Nature has thousands of dimensions: biodiversity, freshwater, soil health, ocean chemistry, pollinator populations, forest cover, and dozens more. That complexity is exactly why your clients need help now, before the frameworks are mandatory and the advice gap becomes a crisis.
What TNFD Actually Requires

TNFD asks organizations to identify, assess, manage, and disclose their nature-related dependencies, impacts, risks, and opportunities. The framework uses a four-step process called LEAP: Locate the interface with nature, Evaluate dependencies and impacts, Assess material risks and opportunities, and Prepare to respond and report. For most mid-market companies, the LEAP process will surface risks they have never formally assessed: supply chain exposure to deforestation, water dependency in drought-prone regions, regulatory risk from biodiversity loss in operating areas, and reputational risk from nature-damaging suppliers.

The TNFD framework was finalized in September 2023 and has already been adopted by over 400 organizations globally as a voluntary standard. The European Union is integrating nature-related disclosures into the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive. The UK is consulting on mandatory TNFD-aligned reporting for listed companies. Canada is watching closely. The window for voluntary adoption before mandatory compliance is shorter than most advisors realize.
Why This Is an Advice Gap, Not Just a Compliance Problem

Most financial advisors, accountants, and industry associations are well-equipped to help clients navigate financial disclosure frameworks. TNFD is different because it requires operational and scientific data that most finance professionals have never worked with. Where does your client source its water? What percentage of its supply chain passes through biodiversity hotspots? Does it operate in or near areas designated as critical natural habitat under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework? These are not questions that a standard financial audit answers.

This is the advice gap. Your clients will come to you with TNFD questions because you are their trusted advisor. If you cannot answer them, or cannot connect them to someone who can, you risk losing the relationship to a competitor who can. The good news is that the gap is closable. You do not need to become a biodiversity expert. You need a partner who can do the nature-risk assessment and give you and your client a clear, financially-framed answer.

The question is not whether your clients will face TNFD requirements. The question is whether you will be the advisor who helps them navigate it, or the one they call after they have already engaged someone else.
The Four Questions Your Clients Will Ask

Based on early TNFD adoption conversations, four questions come up consistently. First: do we have any material nature-related risks? The answer for most mid-market companies is yes, but the location and magnitude vary enormously by sector and geography. Second: what does disclosure actually require us to report? The answer depends on jurisdiction, listing status, and sector, and it is changing. Third: how do we get the data? Most companies do not have nature-related data in their existing systems, and building it from scratch is expensive without the right methodology. Fourth: what should we do about the risks we find? Disclosure without a response plan is a liability, not an asset.

Each of these questions has a defensible answer. The challenge is that the answer requires integrating financial analysis, operational data, supply chain mapping, and nature-science methodology in a way that most single-discipline advisors cannot do alone. That is where the channel partner model becomes valuable: you bring the client relationship and the financial framing, and a specialist partner brings the nature-risk methodology and the data.
What COP17 Means for the Timeline

The Convention on Biological Diversity COP17 is scheduled for late 2026 in Armenia. The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, agreed at COP15 in 2022, committed 196 countries to protecting 30 percent of land and ocean by 2030 and reversing biodiversity loss by 2030. COP17 will assess progress against those commitments and is expected to accelerate mandatory corporate reporting timelines in signatory countries. For your clients, this means the regulatory environment around nature disclosure is tightening, not loosening, and the window to get ahead of it is closing.
Four Actions You Can Take Now

There are four practical steps that financial advisors, accountants, and industry associations can take before TNFD becomes mandatory for their clients. The first is to identify which clients have the highest nature-related exposure: companies in agriculture, food and beverage, mining, construction, pharmaceuticals, and consumer goods are the most exposed sectors globally. The second is to ask those clients whether they have done any nature-risk assessment: most have not, and the question itself signals that you are ahead of the curve. The third is to understand the TNFD LEAP framework at a conceptual level so you can explain it to clients without needing to implement it yourself. The fourth is to establish a referral relationship with a specialist who can do the LEAP assessment and produce a disclosure-ready report.

The Enduring Advantage partner program is designed for exactly this scenario. We do the nature-risk assessment, the TNFD LEAP analysis, and the financially-framed disclosure report. You maintain the client relationship and receive a structured referral arrangement. The client gets a defensible answer to a question that is only going to get more urgent. heldForEditorialReview.title: Water Scarcity: The Corporate Risk That Does Not Show Up on the Balance Sheet
heldForEditorialReview.subtitle: Why water dependency is the next material risk CFOs need to price
heldForEditorialReview.heroAlt: Drought-cracked earth representing water scarcity and corporate water risk
heldForEditorialReview.excerpt: Water is the input your operations cannot replace. As scarcity accelerates, the companies that have mapped their water dependency will have a measurable advantage over those that have not.
heldForEditorialReview.author: Campbell Ohrlis

sections.content: Water does not appear on most corporate balance sheets. It does not have a line in the income statement. It is not tracked as a strategic asset. And yet for a significant proportion of mid-market and enterprise companies, water is the single input that cannot be substituted, relocated, or purchased from an alternative supplier when the primary source fails.

The World Resources Institute estimates that by 2030, global water demand will exceed supply by 40 percent. That is not a distant scenario. It is already happening in parts of the American Southwest, the Indo-Gangetic Plain, the Middle East, and the Mediterranean basin. The companies operating in those regions, or sourcing from them, are already exposed to a risk that their financial statements do not reflect.
What Corporate Water Dependency Actually Means

Water dependency takes three forms. The first is direct operational dependency: manufacturing processes, cooling systems, food and beverage production, data centre cooling, and agricultural operations that require water as a direct input. The second is supply chain dependency: sourcing from regions where key inputs are grown, mined, or processed using water-intensive methods. The third is regulatory dependency: operating in jurisdictions where water use is licensed, and where those licences are subject to curtailment, repricing, or cancellation as scarcity increases.

Each form of dependency creates a different risk profile. Direct operational dependency creates physical risk: the plant stops if the water stops. Supply chain dependency creates cost and availability risk: input prices rise and supply becomes unreliable. Regulatory dependency creates a longer-term structural risk: the licence to operate in a water-stressed region may not be renewable on the same terms in ten years.
The companies that will be most exposed are not those in obviously water-intensive industries. They are the ones that have never asked the question.
The Financial Mechanism: How Water Risk Becomes a Balance Sheet Event

Water risk becomes a financial event through four mechanisms. Production disruption is the most direct: a facility that cannot access water cannot operate. The financial impact is the lost revenue and fixed cost absorption during the disruption, plus the cost of emergency sourcing if available. Input cost inflation is more gradual but more widespread: as water becomes scarcer, the cost of water-intensive agricultural and industrial inputs rises, compressing margins for companies that cannot pass costs through.

Stranded assets are the third mechanism and the most underappreciated. A facility built in a water-abundant region that becomes water-stressed over a 20-year horizon may have significant residual book value but declining operational viability. The impairment risk is real and is not captured in standard financial modelling. The fourth mechanism is regulatory repricing: water that costs almost nothing today in many jurisdictions will be priced at its scarcity value within a decade in the most stressed regions. Companies that have not modelled this repricing into their long-term cost structures are carrying an unquantified liability.
The TNFD Connection: Water as a Nature-Related Financial Risk

The Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures explicitly includes freshwater as a critical natural system. The TNFD LEAP framework asks companies to locate their interface with freshwater systems, evaluate their dependencies and impacts, assess material risks, and prepare to respond and report. For most companies, the freshwater assessment will be the most material output of the TNFD process, because freshwater dependency is more operationally direct than biodiversity dependency for most business models.

The connection between TNFD and water risk means that companies preparing for nature-related disclosure requirements will need a water dependency map as a foundational input. That map does not exist in most organizations today. Building it requires combining operational data, supply chain geography, and hydrological data in a way that most finance teams have not done before.
What a Water Risk Assessment Covers

A structured water risk assessment covers four areas. The first is a water dependency inventory: which operations, processes, and supply chain nodes use water, at what volume, and from which sources. The second is a water stress mapping: overlaying the dependency inventory against current and projected water stress levels using tools like the WRI Aqueduct Water Risk Atlas. The third is a financial exposure quantification: translating the stress mapping into financial scenarios covering production disruption, input cost inflation, regulatory repricing, and asset impairment. The fourth is a response prioritization: ranking the identified risks by financial materiality and identifying the highest-return mitigation actions.

The response options range from operational efficiency measures (reducing water consumption per unit of output) to supply chain diversification (sourcing from less water-stressed regions) to on-site water recycling and storage infrastructure to engagement with watershed governance bodies. Each option has a different cost, timeline, and risk-reduction profile. The prioritization process is the same as any other sustainability investment decision: rank by financial return, implement in order, measure and verify.
The CFO Question: Where Do We Start?

The starting point for most organizations is a water dependency inventory combined with a stress mapping. This does not require a full TNFD assessment. It requires knowing which of your operations and supply chain nodes are in water-stressed regions, and what the financial exposure would be if water availability declined by 20 percent, 40 percent, or became subject to significant repricing. That analysis can be done in a structured triage process, and the output is a prioritized exposure view with financial estimates attached.

Bring us your operations footprint and your key supply chain geographies. We will tell you where the biggest water-related exposures are and what they are worth to address.

heldForEditorialReview.subtitle: The financial case for layered location risk assessment before your next capital decision.
heldForEditorialReview.author: Campbell Ohrlis
heldForEditorialReview.heroAlt: Aerial view of a coastal city at dusk, illustrating location risk layers
heldForEditorialReview.excerpt: Hurricane exposure. Sea-level rise. Freshwater availability. Wildfire probability. Every location sits at a unique intersection of these risk layers. Most organizations look at one layer at a time. The ones that look at all four together are making better capital decisions.

sections.content: Think of it as layering heat maps. One layer for hurricane exposure. One for sea-level rise. One for freshwater availability. One for wildfire probability. Every location has its own unique configuration of risk layers, and the combination tells a very different story than any single layer alone.

Most organizations do location risk analysis one layer at a time, if they do it at all. They commission a flood study for a specific site after a near-miss event. They review their insurance coverage after a wildfire season. They notice that a key supplier is in a water-stressed region after a production disruption. Each of these is a reactive response to a single layer.

The organizations that are making better capital decisions are doing something different. They are building a composite picture of each location before they commit capital, not after. They are asking: what is the combined risk profile of this site across all four layers, and how does that profile change over a 10-year, 20-year, and 30-year horizon?
The Four Layers

Hurricane exposure is the most familiar layer for organizations with operations in coastal regions. The risk is not just direct physical damage. It is the cumulative cost of business interruption, supply chain disruption, and the increasing difficulty of obtaining affordable insurance as insurers reprice their own exposure. State Farm and Allstate stopped writing new homeowner policies in California in 2023. The properties affected had not burned. They were simply located where enough people expected fire. The same dynamic is playing out in Florida, Louisiana, and coastal Texas for hurricane risk.

Sea-level rise operates on a longer timeline but with a financial mechanism that is already active. Property values in coastal areas begin to decline when a critical mass of buyers, lenders, and insurers expect flooding, not when flooding actually occurs. Research from the First Street Foundation shows that flood risk is already being priced into property values in affected markets, with discounts of 5 to 15 percent in the most exposed areas. For organizations with significant real estate holdings or long-term lease commitments in coastal locations, this is a balance sheet risk that does not require a flood to materialize.

Freshwater availability is the least visible layer for most organizations, but it is the one with the most direct operational consequence. The WRI Aqueduct Water Risk Atlas projects that by 2030, 40 percent of the global population will live in areas of high water stress. For manufacturing, food processing, data centres, and agricultural operations, water availability is a direct constraint on production capacity. Organizations that have mapped their freshwater dependency against projected stress levels are finding material exposure in locations they considered low-risk.

Wildfire probability has moved from a regional concern to a global one. The 2021 Lytton, British Columbia wildfire destroyed a town of 1,000 people in a region that had never experienced significant wildfire risk. The 2022 Gironde fires in France burned through wine country that had been producing for centuries. The 2023 Maui fires destroyed Lahaina, a historic town that had not been in any wildfire risk model. The pattern is consistent: the risk is expanding faster than the models, and the financial consequences arrive before the models catch up.
Why the Combination Matters More Than Any Single Layer

A site that scores moderate on each individual layer may score very high on the composite. A manufacturing facility in a coastal region with moderate hurricane exposure, moderate sea-level rise risk, and moderate freshwater stress is not a moderate-risk facility. It is a facility where three separate risk mechanisms are operating simultaneously, each capable of triggering the others.

The 2012 Thailand floods illustrate this dynamic. A single flooding event disrupted global hard drive supply chains for 18 months because a cluster of manufacturing facilities in the Chao Phraya river basin were simultaneously affected. Each facility had been assessed individually. None had been assessed as part of a supply chain concentration risk. The composite picture was invisible until it became a crisis.

The same logic applies to the Fargo, North Dakota flood insurance market. Fargo sits on the Red River, which flows north and is prone to ice-jam flooding in spring. In 2009, a major flood event caused $2 billion in damage. Property values in the flood plain had not reflected this risk before the event. After the event, flood insurance premiums in the area increased by 300 to 500 percent for properties in the highest-risk zones. The financial consequence arrived not with the flood, but with the repricing of risk that followed.
The Capital Decision Implication

For a CFO making a capital allocation decision about a new facility, a long-term lease, or a major supply chain commitment, the composite location risk profile is a material input. It affects the expected useful life of the asset, the cost of insuring it, the availability of financing for it, and the residual value at the end of the commitment period.

The organizations that are building this composite picture before they commit are not doing so because they are more environmentally conscious. They are doing so because they have learned, usually from a painful experience, that single-layer risk assessment misses the interactions between layers that drive the largest financial consequences.

The good news is that the data to build this composite picture exists. Hurricane track databases, sea-level rise projections, freshwater stress atlases, and wildfire probability models are all publicly available. The challenge is not data availability. The challenge is integrating four separate data sources into a single decision-relevant picture for each location in your portfolio.
What a Composite Location Risk Assessment Covers

A structured composite location risk assessment covers four steps. First, inventory: identify every location in your operations and supply chain that represents a material capital commitment or operational dependency. Second, layer mapping: overlay each location against current and projected risk levels for all four layers using best-available data sources. Third, composite scoring: combine the four layers into a single risk score for each location, weighted by the financial exposure at that location. Fourth, response prioritization: rank the identified risks by financial materiality and identify the highest-return mitigation actions, which may include physical hardening, insurance restructuring, supply chain diversification, or exit from the highest-risk locations.

The output is not a report. It is a prioritized view of locations by composite risk, with financial exposure estimates attached to each. That view is the input to a capital allocation conversation, not an environmental compliance exercise.
The CFO Question: Where Do We Start?

The starting point for most organizations is a location inventory combined with a composite risk mapping for the top 20 percent of locations by capital exposure. This does not require a full climate risk assessment. It requires knowing which of your locations are in the highest-risk zones across all four layers, and what the financial exposure would be if those risks materialized on a 10-year horizon.

heldForEditorialReview.author: Campbell Ohrlis
heldForEditorialReview.heroAlt: Close-up of rich agricultural soil with a seedling, representing soil health and land productivity
heldForEditorialReview.excerpt: UNCCD’s 2022 Global Land Outlook reports that up to 40 percent of the world’s land is degraded. For food and beverage companies, pharmaceutical manufacturers, and organizations with agricultural supply chains, that is a balance-sheet risk hiding in plain sight.

sections.content: UNCCD’s 2022 Global Land Outlook reports that up to 40 percent of the world’s land is degraded. For most CFOs, land degradation can sit in a different mental category from the financial risks they manage daily. It should not.

Soil health is a supply chain risk. It is a raw material availability risk. It is an input cost risk. And for organizations that own or lease agricultural land, it is a direct asset impairment risk. The financial mechanism is not abstract. It is the same mechanism that drives any commodity supply disruption: when productive capacity declines, prices rise, availability tightens, and organizations that have not diversified their sourcing face margin compression or production constraints.
How Soil Degradation Becomes a Financial Event

Soil degradation reduces agricultural productivity through four mechanisms. Erosion removes the topsoil layer that contains most of the organic matter and nutrients that support plant growth. Compaction reduces the soil's ability to absorb water and support root development. Salinization from irrigation and fertilizer use makes soil increasingly inhospitable to crops. And the loss of soil biodiversity, specifically the microbial communities that cycle nutrients and support plant health, reduces the soil's ability to support productive agriculture without increasing chemical inputs.

Each of these mechanisms translates directly into financial outcomes. Lower yields mean higher cost per unit of output. Increasing chemical inputs to compensate for lost soil fertility means higher input costs. Irrigation to compensate for reduced water retention means higher water costs and greater exposure to water scarcity risk. And when a region's agricultural productivity declines below the threshold where farming is economically viable, the supply chain disruption is not gradual. It is a step change.

The 2022 Pakistan floods illustrate the step-change dynamic. Pakistan produces 70 percent of the world's cotton supply. The 2022 floods, which were made significantly more severe by degraded soil in the Indus River basin that could not absorb the rainfall, destroyed 45 percent of Pakistan's cotton crop. Global cotton prices spiked 40 percent in three months. Apparel manufacturers that had not diversified their cotton sourcing faced immediate margin pressure. The soil degradation that contributed to the flood severity had been documented for decades. The financial consequence arrived in a single season.
The Industries Most Exposed

Food and beverage companies are the most directly exposed. For manufacturers of products that depend on specific agricultural commodities, soil degradation in key growing regions is an existential supply chain risk. Chocolate manufacturers dependent on West African cocoa, coffee companies dependent on Central American arabica, and wine producers dependent on specific terroir are all exposed to the productivity decline of specific soil ecosystems.

Pharmaceutical companies are less obviously exposed but equally vulnerable. Approximately 25 percent of pharmaceutical compounds are derived from plant sources, and many of the plants used in pharmaceutical production are cultivated in regions experiencing significant land degradation. The supply chains for botanical ingredients are often less diversified than food supply chains, making them more vulnerable to regional productivity shocks.

Agricultural input companies face a different version of the same risk. As soil health declines, demand for fertilizers, pesticides, and irrigation equipment increases in the short term, creating apparent revenue growth. But the long-term trajectory is toward a productivity collapse that eliminates the customer base. Companies in this sector that are not investing in soil health restoration are harvesting short-term revenue at the cost of their long-term market.

Real estate and infrastructure companies with holdings in agricultural regions face direct asset impairment risk. Land that is currently productive agricultural land may become unproductive within a 20 to 30 year horizon if current degradation trends continue. For long-term infrastructure investments in regions dependent on agricultural economic activity, the soil health trajectory of the surrounding region is a material input to the investment thesis.
The TNFD Connection

The Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures framework explicitly includes soil health and land degradation as material nature-related risks. Under the TNFD LEAP framework, organizations are required to locate their dependencies on ecosystem services, evaluate their exposure to nature-related risks, assess the materiality of those risks, and prepare disclosure. For organizations with agricultural supply chains, soil health is one of the most material ecosystem service dependencies they have.

The TNFD disclosure requirements are moving from voluntary to mandatory in multiple jurisdictions. The EU Nature Restoration Law, the UK Biodiversity Net Gain requirements, and the emerging mandatory TNFD frameworks in Australia and Canada are all creating regulatory pressure for organizations to understand and disclose their nature-related dependencies. For CFOs who have not yet mapped their soil health exposure, the regulatory timeline is now short enough that this is a near-term compliance risk as well as a long-term supply chain risk.
What a Soil Health Risk Assessment Covers

A structured soil health risk assessment covers three areas. The first is a supply chain mapping: identifying which agricultural commodities are material inputs to the organization's products or operations, and where those commodities are grown. The second is a degradation exposure assessment: overlaying the supply chain geography against current soil health data and degradation trend projections to identify which supply chain nodes are in high-risk regions. The third is a financial exposure quantification: translating the degradation exposure into financial scenarios covering input cost inflation, supply availability constraints, and regulatory repricing.

The response options range from supply chain diversification (sourcing from less degraded regions) to supplier engagement programs (working with key suppliers on soil health restoration practices) to direct investment in regenerative agriculture (which can qualify for green financing and generate carbon credits as a co-benefit) to product reformulation (reducing dependence on the most at-risk commodities).
The CFO Question: Where Do We Start?

The starting point is a supply chain mapping combined with a degradation exposure assessment for the top 20 percent of agricultural inputs by spend. This does not require a full TNFD assessment. It requires knowing which of your key agricultural supply chain nodes are in regions with declining soil health, and what the financial exposure would be if productivity in those regions declined by 20 percent over the next decade.

heldForEditorialReview.title: Ocean Acidification: The Marine Supply Chain Risk Most CFOs Have Never Priced
heldForEditorialReview.subtitle: The ocean absorbs a third of the carbon dioxide we emit. The chemistry is changing faster than most supply chain models account for, and the financial exposure is not limited to seafood companies.
heldForEditorialReview.author: Campbell Ohrlis
heldForEditorialReview.heroAlt: Working shellfish harbour with vessels, crates, and cold-chain loading infrastructure
heldForEditorialReview.excerpt: NOAA reports that the ocean absorbs about 30 percent of carbon dioxide released to the atmosphere. Surface-ocean pH has fallen by 0.1 units since the Industrial Revolution, approximately a 30 percent increase in acidity. For CFOs who think this is a problem for marine biologists, the supply chain exposure is closer than they expect.

sections.content: The Chemistry Is Not Complicated

NOAA reports that the ocean absorbs about 30 percent of carbon dioxide released to the atmosphere. As that carbon dioxide dissolves, it forms carbonic acid. In the 200-plus years since the Industrial Revolution began, surface-ocean pH has fallen by 0.1 pH units, approximately a 30 percent increase in acidity (NOAA, 2026).

The financial mechanism is straightforward. More acidic water makes it harder for marine organisms to build calcium carbonate shells and skeletons. Oysters, mussels, clams, sea urchins, coral, and the tiny pteropods that form the base of many marine food webs all depend on calcium carbonate. When the water becomes too acidic, shells dissolve faster than they can be built. Juvenile shellfish are particularly vulnerable: Pacific oyster larvae in the Pacific Northwest began showing mass die-offs in the mid-2000s, traced directly to upwelling of more acidic deep water.
The Supply Chain Exposure Is Not Limited to Seafood

The obvious exposure is in seafood supply chains. Global aquaculture produces roughly 90 million tonnes of seafood per year, with shellfish and molluscs representing a significant share. Companies with seafood in their supply chains, whether as a direct product or as an ingredient in processed foods, face input cost inflation and supply availability risk as aquaculture yields become more volatile.

The less obvious exposure is in the pharmaceutical and nutraceutical industries. Marine organisms are the source of a significant number of pharmaceutical compounds, including antibiotics, anticoagulants, and cancer treatments. Coral reefs alone are estimated to have contributed to the development of over 20 approved drugs. As reef ecosystems degrade, the biodiversity that underpins future drug discovery contracts.

Coastal tourism and hospitality companies face a third exposure. Coral reef tourism generates an estimated $36 billion per year globally. The Great Barrier Reef alone contributes approximately $6.4 billion annually to the Australian economy. As bleaching events become more frequent and severe, the asset base that underpins this revenue is being degraded. For hotel groups, resort operators, and travel companies with significant coastal exposure, the reef degradation timeline is a long-term revenue risk.
The Insurance and Financing Dimension

Coastal infrastructure insurers are beginning to price reef degradation into their models. Coral reefs provide natural wave attenuation that reduces the energy of storm surges reaching coastal properties. A 2018 study in Nature Communications estimated that reefs reduce wave energy by 97 percent on average. As reefs degrade, the cost of insuring coastal properties increases, and in some cases insurance becomes unavailable at any price.

Green bond and sustainability-linked loan frameworks are increasingly incorporating ocean health metrics. The Blue Economy Finance Principles, backed by major development banks, are creating a framework for ocean-linked financing that rewards companies with demonstrable positive impact on marine ecosystems. Companies that can demonstrate reduced ocean impact may access preferential financing terms; those that cannot will face higher capital costs as the framework matures.
The TNFD Connection

The Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures framework explicitly includes ocean and marine ecosystems as material nature-related risk categories. Under the TNFD LEAP framework, organizations are required to assess their dependencies on ocean ecosystem services, including fisheries, coastal protection, and marine biodiversity. For companies with any coastal or marine exposure, the TNFD disclosure requirements create a near-term compliance obligation to understand and quantify this risk.

The EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive and the emerging mandatory TNFD frameworks in the UK, Australia, and Canada are all creating regulatory pressure for organizations to disclose their nature-related dependencies. Ocean acidification sits squarely within the scope of these requirements. CFOs who have not yet mapped their marine ecosystem dependencies are building a compliance gap that will need to be closed on a compressed timeline.
What a Marine Risk Assessment Covers

A structured marine risk assessment covers four areas. The first is supply chain mapping: identifying which products, ingredients, or raw materials have direct or indirect marine dependencies. The second is geographic exposure: determining which supply chain nodes are in regions where ocean acidification, warming, or deoxygenation is already affecting productivity. The third is financial exposure quantification: translating the geographic exposure into financial scenarios covering input cost inflation, supply availability constraints, and regulatory repricing. The fourth is opportunity identification: mapping which marine ecosystem restoration investments qualify for green financing and generate measurable co-benefits.
The CFO Question: Where Do We Start?

The starting point is a supply chain mapping focused on marine dependencies: seafood ingredients, pharmaceutical compounds, coastal infrastructure, and tourism assets. This does not require a full TNFD assessment. It requires knowing which of your key supply chain nodes have marine ecosystem dependencies, and what the financial exposure would be if productivity in those ecosystems declined by 20 percent over the next decade.

Bring us your key marine dependencies and your coastal asset exposure. We'll tell you where the biggest ocean-related exposures are and what they're worth to address.

heldForEditorialReview.title: Every Sustainability Solution Works Somewhere. How Do You Find the One That Works Here?
heldForEditorialReview.subtitle: The hard problem is not finding an option. It is choosing the one that belongs first in your operation, under your financial and operating constraints.
heldForEditorialReview.author: Campbell Ohrlis
heldForEditorialReview.authorBio: Campbell Ohrlis works with leadership teams on the commercial question underneath sustainability: where exposure is material, what can be influenced, and which decision belongs first.
heldForEditorialReview.heroAlt: Physical comparison of technical proposals and operating evidence
heldForEditorialReview.excerpt: Thousands of credible options exist. The scarce resource is a disciplined way to decide which one belongs first in your company.
heldForEditorialReview.linkedInExcerpt: Every sustainability solution works somewhere. The question is whether it is the best use of your next dollar, in your buildings, on your line, under your capital constraints. The market is not short of options. It is short of a way to choose between them.

faq.question: What should a strong first recommendation include?
faq.answer: It should name one next action, show financial return and environmental impact together, state what was screened out and why, and be clear about assumptions and confidence.

faq.question: Can useful advice start before data is complete?
faq.answer: Yes. A credible first phase starts with available data or a real funding and operating decision, then refines the picture as better information becomes available.

faq.question: Why ask about equipment sales and referral fees?
faq.answer: Independence is structural. Buyers should understand whether the advisor benefits from a particular product, vendor relationship, or affiliated technology before relying on the recommendation.

sections.content:
Hundreds of billions of dollars have gone into technologies, programs, and services addressing climate, biodiversity loss, and pollution. That investment produced thousands of credible options. Most work somewhere.

That is precisely why choice is difficult. The chance that any one option is the best use of your next dollar, in your buildings or on your production line, given your equipment ages and capital constraints, is small. You are not short of options. You are short of a way to choose between them.
Ask for the next action, and what was screened out

A weak answer is a long menu, a scoring matrix nobody can explain, or a recommendation to create another working group. A strong answer names one action, shows financial return and environmental impact together, and explains what was excluded and why.

Materiality is the filter. If an option is not material to your company, it should not consume the decision-maker’s attention. The practical test is whether the recommendation can be defended when finance, operations, and a skeptical executive ask why it outranked the alternatives.
Start with what you know, not with a promise to assess everything

Almost no company has complete data on day one. A sensible approach starts where records, funding, or an operational decision already exist, produces an early result that can be tested, and uses that progress to sharpen the next decision.

Ask what the first phase can establish with the data available now, what would confirm or change the initial view, and which data gaps actually matter. A broad whole-field view can develop as the information compounds. It does not have to delay the first useful move.
Test independence and the human check

Ask directly whether the advisor sells equipment, takes referral fees, or has affiliated technology and ownership relationships. Related arrangements are not automatically a problem. Undisclosed incentives are. A vendor can see a genuine problem and still have a predictable shape to its recommendation.

Generative tools can accelerate a detailed draft. They cannot confirm local contractor capacity, actual site conditions, or a funding window that has already closed. Ask who reviews the analysis before it reaches you, what field experience they bring, and what they would change after a site-level sanity test.
A good first conversation leaves you with a credible next action, the information that would confirm it, and a clearer view of what the first phase must prove.

heldForEditorialReview.title: What Is the Right Order Actually Worth?
heldForEditorialReview.subtitle: The return on sequencing can exceed the return on any individual project, because the right order protects capital, timing, and the ability to fund what comes next.
heldForEditorialReview.author: Campbell Ohrlis
heldForEditorialReview.authorBio: Campbell Ohrlis works with leadership teams on the commercial question underneath sustainability: where exposure is material, what can be influenced, and which decision belongs first.
heldForEditorialReview.heroAlt: Financial review of capital allocation papers, utility invoices, and material samples
heldForEditorialReview.excerpt: The order of otherwise credible projects can determine whether a program compounds value or simply spends capital.
heldForEditorialReview.linkedInExcerpt: The biggest return is often not inside a project. It is inside the order of the projects. Timing a decision against equipment cycles, funding windows, and operating constraints can protect more value than choosing a different technology.

faq.question: Why does sequencing matter in sustainability investment?
faq.answer: Projects can be individually credible but collectively underperform if they are mistimed, duplicate work, consume capital needed for a stronger option, or depend on an asset that is about to be replaced.

faq.question: Should incentives determine the project order?
faq.answer: Incentives can improve an already sound project. They should not be the sole reason to choose an option that fails the organization’s own financial criteria without support.

faq.question: What should finance require before approving a first action?
faq.answer: A clear recommendation, economics with and without incentives, stated assumptions, an agreed baseline method, delivery ownership, and a realistic plan for verification.

sections.content:
Two organizations can commit the same capital to environmental improvements and end up with very different results. The difference is often not the technology. It is the order.

A visible project may arrive first because a vendor called, a grant is expiring, or it is easy to explain to a board. Yet controls, maintenance, process changes, or a project aligned to an equipment replacement cycle may produce a stronger financial result with less disruption. Sequencing is a capital-allocation decision dressed in engineering language.
Where order decides the outcome

The right asset installed too early can lose much of its value when the equipment it depends on is replaced soon after. A visible initiative can consume capital that would have been better used on operational work. A project can miss a funding window because no one aligned the schedule. And a program that only works on a subsidy can become fragile when rules change.

The more useful question is not “Does this option work?” It is “Does it belong ahead of the other credible options, given our asset cycles, financial criteria, operating constraints, and current source of risk?”
Why the exposure is becoming more material

CDP reported in May 2026 that 11,261 companies disclosing full environmental data in 2025 anticipated US$714 billion in future financial impacts from extreme weather, with 48% of identified risks expected within two years. CDP also reported a median mitigation cost of US$3.1 million against a median risk cost of US$39.4 million.

A 2024 Nature study, summarised by King’s College London, estimated that climate disruption to global supply chains could contribute US$3.75 trillion to US$24.7 trillion in net economic losses in 2020 dollars by 2060 depending on the emissions pathway. These are system-level figures, not a forecast for an individual company. They underline why the first decision should account for operating, supply-chain, and capital risk together.
