sections.content: The comparison that matters

The usual comparison is advisory cost against savings. A more useful comparison is the cost of a disciplined decision process against the cost of spending capital in the wrong order.

There are times when a formal sequencing exercise is not the right purchase. A single-site organization with modest spend, no funding capacity, or a narrow compliance request may be better served by a focused technical audit or internal action. The work earns its place when multiple material choices, timing constraints, and external scrutiny make the order consequential.
Sources and context

Sources: CDP, “Extreme Weather Risk is Reshaping the Global Economy,” 12 May 2026; Wang et al., “Global supply chains amplify economic costs of future extreme heat risk,” Nature, 2024; and Verdantix, “ESG And Sustainability Consulting: Market Size and Forecast 2021-2027,” 2022. Verdantix’s US$16 billion 2027 projection was a historical forecast, not a current market-size estimate.

heldForEditorialReview.title: How Do You Get From Thousands of Options to One Funded Decision?
heldForEditorialReview.subtitle: A better sequence begins with the actual decision, uses available data honestly, and tests whether an advisor can help narrow the field before it becomes another report.
heldForEditorialReview.author: Campbell Ohrlis
heldForEditorialReview.authorBio: Campbell Ohrlis works with leadership teams on the commercial question underneath sustainability: where exposure is material, what can be influenced, and which decision belongs first.
heldForEditorialReview.heroAlt: Independent advisor checking a vendor proposal against site evidence
heldForEditorialReview.excerpt: A broad request for proposal can produce polished answers and less clarity. Start with the decision you need made and ask for a credible first move.
heldForEditorialReview.linkedInExcerpt: Most companies outsource the hardest part of sustainability to a procurement process: deciding what goes first. Start instead with one sentence describing the decision. Then test whether an advisor can offer a defensible first hypothesis, explain what would change it, and stay accountable to delivery.

faq.question: What should be in a sustainability advisory brief?
faq.answer: State the decision you need made, the data already available, relevant capital and timing constraints, and the people who must be able to defend the next action.

faq.question: How many firms should we shortlist?
faq.answer: A focused shortlist is often more useful than a wide proposal process. The goal is to compare reasoning, independence, and delivery fit rather than merely score credentials.

faq.question: What should a first engagement prove?
faq.answer: It should demonstrate whether the work can change the next decision by producing a recommendation, transparent assumptions, an agreed baseline method, and a clear ownership path.

sections.content:
Many companies start backwards. They write a broad scope, send it to several firms, compare proposals, and select the one that appears most comprehensive. Months later, they can have a polished document and no more clarity about what should happen first.

The decision itself is the hard part. A procurement process is useful for comparing defined work. It is not designed to define the first material action in a field of unlike options.
The cost of narrowing too early

Think of it like standing in a museum. Step back far enough and you see everything. Zoom in too early and you miss most of it.

A wide view keeps credible alternatives visible before the detailed work begins. Narrowing too early can hide the decision that matters most. actio starts with the whole field and screens out what is not material, grounded in your data and the market context.

Everyone knows the feeling of scrolling Netflix all evening and never picking a movie. Wasting an evening is fine. Wasting years, and billions of dollars, dithering on a sustainability decision destroys ecosystems and balance sheets. Decision paralysis has real cost here.
Write down the decision, not the project

Put the actual decision in one sentence. Not “develop a sustainability strategy.” Something closer to “we have capital available and no defensible way to rank the projects competing for it,” or “two major customers have requirements we cannot yet answer.”

Then take a short inventory of what you already know: utility records, equipment ages, metering, water and waste invoices, previous audits, fleet information, and production volumes. The data will be incomplete. That is normal. It tells you what can be answered in the first phase and what must be refined later.
Understand the type of help you are buying

Technical specialists are valuable when the project is already known. Reporting firms are valuable when a customer or regulator requires a specific document. Large integrated firms can bring breadth. An independent decision partner is useful when the question is what goes first and how to coordinate the specialists after that choice is made.

A focused shortlist should test fit, not create a theatre of comparison. Ask each firm what it thinks the next action might be based on the information provided, what would confirm or disprove that view, and what it would screen out first.
Use the first meeting as a test

Bring finance and operations. Ask what the firm would do before the data is complete, who reviews the work before it reaches you, what it has advised against in a similar context, and whether it sells equipment or takes referral fees.

The point is not to demand certainty from a first conversation. It is to see whether the advisor can reason in public, distinguish a hypothesis from a promise, disclose incentives, and describe how a recommendation becomes a plan somebody will run.
A first phase should prove that the work changes the next decision, not merely that the advisor can produce a longer document.

heldForEditorialReview.title: Can Our Own Team Work Out What Goes First?
heldForEditorialReview.subtitle: Internal teams should own the operational work they can do well. Outside support becomes useful when unlike options, capital timing, independent comparison, and verification make the choice harder.
heldForEditorialReview.author: Campbell Ohrlis
heldForEditorialReview.authorBio: Campbell Ohrlis works with leadership teams on the commercial question underneath sustainability: where exposure is material, what can be influenced, and which decision belongs first.
heldForEditorialReview.heroAlt: Commercial facility maintenance inspection with operating equipment and field notes
heldForEditorialReview.excerpt: Your team can often identify obvious waste. The harder question is when choices become unlike enough that a disciplined external comparison is worth paying for.
heldForEditorialReview.linkedInExcerpt: Some of the best environmental returns are available to internal teams with a utility portal, a spreadsheet, and operating knowledge. Do that work first. Bring in outside help when the question changes from finding opportunities to choosing between unlike options under capital, timing, and verification constraints.

faq.question: What sustainability work can an internal team do well?
faq.answer: Internal teams are often best placed to find obvious operational waste, gather records, review bills, maintain operating discipline, and complete straightforward customer questionnaires.

faq.question: When does external support add value?
faq.answer: It is most useful when leaders must compare unlike initiatives, evaluate vendors independently, sequence work against asset cycles, build a verification method, or create capacity to carry a decision through delivery.

faq.question: Can an internal team and advisor work together?
faq.answer: Yes. A productive division is for the company to own its data, operating knowledge, and execution relationships while external support contributes prioritisation, independent comparison, and verification discipline.

sections.content:
For a meaningful share of the work, the answer is yes. Your people may be the best people to find compressed-air leaks, equipment operating through unoccupied hours, billing errors, weak schedules, and the records needed to understand the baseline. That work should not be outsourced simply because it carries a sustainability label.

The line is not between simple and hard work. It is between finding opportunities and choosing between them.
What internal teams do better than anyone outside

Maintenance and operations teams know the site, the constraints, and the habits that influence performance. They can review utility bills and tariffs, collect equipment information, assemble production records, complete basic questionnaires, and maintain the routines that keep improvements in place.

Doing this work early improves the operating picture and makes later specialist input more efficient. You are not paying advisory rates for data entry, and the organization develops a clearer view of the conditions any recommendation must respect.
Where internal effort runs out of road

The difficulty changes when a heat-recovery project, fleet transition, refrigerant change, and packaging redesign each have different financial profiles, risks, environmental effects, and operating implications. Ranking them needs a method, not a meeting.

The same is true of vendor evaluation, timing a project against replacement cycles, documenting a result others will trust, and managing funding windows. The constraint is often attention. An operations lead with a full role can identify the opportunity yet still lack the time to compare quotes, coordinate specialists, hold a schedule, and report to leadership.
A short decision test

Can you name the highest-value next action and defend the ranking against finance? Does someone have real capacity to run the work? Are the options comparable enough to assess internally? Is the capital or external scrutiny significant enough that the order matters?

When the answers are clear, keep going. When several are not, a hybrid model often works best: the internal team owns data, operating discipline, and delivery relationships, while outside support contributes prioritisation, independent comparison, and a verification method.

heldForEditorialReview.title: What Does an Actionable Sustainability Plan Actually Contain?
heldForEditorialReview.subtitle: A plan is not an inventory, framework, or ranked menu. It is a clear next action, the conditions for delivery, and a way to know whether the result arrived.
heldForEditorialReview.author: Campbell Ohrlis
heldForEditorialReview.authorBio: Campbell Ohrlis works with leadership teams on the commercial question underneath sustainability: where exposure is material, what can be influenced, and which decision belongs first.
heldForEditorialReview.heroAlt: Specialists reviewing an implementation checklist at a manufacturing loading dock
heldForEditorialReview.excerpt: An actionable plan makes the crowded field smaller. It establishes what is happening, names the next action, attaches the delivery conditions, and states how the result will be verified.
heldForEditorialReview.linkedInExcerpt: A sustainability plan is not a long report. It is a picture of what is happening, one recommended next action, a delivery plan someone owns, independent vendor comparison, appropriate funding support, and a verification method agreed before work begins.

faq.question: What is the difference between a sustainability plan and a report?
faq.answer: A plan names a next action, states what was screened out, makes assumptions visible, assigns delivery ownership, and explains how results will be measured. A report may describe options without reducing the decision.

faq.question: Should incentives drive the recommendation?
faq.answer: Incentives should improve projects that already make financial and operational sense. They should not be the only reason a project is selected.

faq.question: Why agree verification before implementation?
faq.answer: A written baseline and measurement method help distinguish an estimate from a result and give finance, customers, or lenders a shared basis for evaluating performance.

sections.content:
Ask ten firms for a sustainability plan and you may receive ten documents that differ radically in scope and price. Some are inventories. Some are frameworks. Some are ranked menus with a proposal for a later phase. Very few tell you what to do on Monday.

A plan worth acting on contains the information needed to make, deliver, and test one decision. It narrows the field rather than expanding it.
A picture of what is really happening

Start with where energy, water, materials, and waste are going, what they cost, and how performance compares with what the operation should reasonably require. Utility records, equipment age and condition, spend by site and end use, and relevant production information form the input.

The valuable output is not the inventory. It is the variance. When comparable sites or processes perform differently, the gap is where the decision becomes interesting.
One recommended next action

Anyone can produce a list of opportunities. A real plan screens out what is not material and names the single next action that best fits the organization’s financial criteria, operating reality, and environmental objectives.

The recommendation should include visible reasoning, expected value with stated confidence, the material alternatives excluded, and economics with and without incentives. If the ranking cannot stand up to finance, it is not yet a decision.
A delivery path and vendor process

A recommendation is not a plan until it includes the specification, qualified bidder approach, total-cost comparison, budget, schedule against asset cycles and operating windows, and a named internal owner.

Technology can accelerate a first draft. A human review still has to test contractor capacity, program rules, local conditions, and operational reality. The vendor process should be written for the company’s situation rather than around a seller’s product, and the comparison should extend beyond sticker price.
Funding, verification, and accountability

Funding can improve a project that already makes sense. An eligibility screen, application support, and reporting requirements should be attached to the actual project list, not treated as a reason to choose a weaker project.

A written baseline, stated measurement method, and periodic reporting distinguish claimed savings from verified results. Someone also has to hold the schedule, follow up with vendors, escalate delays, and report to leadership. A sound plan without delivery ownership becomes a folder.
The test is simple: did the crowded field of options get smaller by the time you finished reading?

heldForEditorialReview.title: How Fast Can You Know What to Do Next?
heldForEditorialReview.subtitle: Time to a defensible decision, time to implementation, and time to verified results are different clocks. A credible program names each one plainly.
heldForEditorialReview.author: Campbell Ohrlis
heldForEditorialReview.authorBio: Campbell Ohrlis works with leadership teams on the commercial question underneath sustainability: where exposure is material, what can be influenced, and which decision belongs first.
heldForEditorialReview.heroAlt: Operations planning wall with work orders, a site map, and timeline markers
heldForEditorialReview.excerpt: A useful decision can emerge in weeks. Implementation and verification follow different calendars. The plan should make those clocks visible rather than collapsing them into one promise.
heldForEditorialReview.linkedInExcerpt: How fast can you know what to do next? Time to a defensible decision is often measured in weeks. Time to implementation and a result finance can rely on follows different clocks. A credible plan separates them instead of offering one number that means three things.

faq.question: How quickly can a company identify a first action?
faq.answer: With a clear decision scope and usable records, a focused first phase can often identify a defensible next action in weeks. Timing depends on data access, number of sites, and decision complexity.

faq.question: Why do verified results take longer?
faq.answer: Procurement, equipment lead times, operating windows, permits, seasonality, and the need for sufficient post-project data can extend the time required to confirm a result.

faq.question: What speeds up a program?
faq.answer: A named internal data owner, decision-maker access, existing metering or records, capital already approved in principle, and early checks of funding and procurement calendars can all reduce avoidable delay.

sections.content:
Three different questions hide inside “how fast can you know what to do next?” Time to a defensible decision, time to implemented action, and time to a result finance can rely on are not the same.

Trouble starts when someone quotes the first number and delivers against the third, or when a buyer expects the third and is sold only the first. A credible program separates the clocks.
First, establish what data exists

Utility records, equipment registers, production volumes, previous audits, existing metering, and targeted site visits can establish a useful starting point. The delay is often not analysis. It is waiting for internal records. Naming a data owner before work begins can remove more delay than adding people to the project team.

The first decision phase then normalises useful data, compares sites or processes where appropriate, screens out what is not material, and produces a recommended action with stated assumptions. The aim is not to assess everything immediately. It is to identify the first move.
Then turn the decision into a plan

Specifications, bidder lists, real quotes, total-cost comparison, funding applications, internal approvals, and a schedule against operational windows all take time. Drafting can be faster with technology. Human review, contractor capacity, site conditions, and procurement calendars do not compress in the same way.

Controls and operational changes can often move sooner. Larger electrical or mechanical projects may be governed by lead times, permits, utility interconnection, or shutdown windows. The plan should make those dependencies visible before a promise is made.
Finally, verify the result

Weather, production, and seasonality can make early results indicative rather than conclusive. A written starting point and measurement method agreed before implementation help finance distinguish early signals from a result that has been tested over a relevant operating period.

The most useful schedule starts where information or a credible opportunity already exists, sequences a practical early win beside longer capital work, and sets decision gates that ask whether the work has changed what happens next.
A realistic program does not promise that every result arrives at once. It shows what is knowable now, what can move next, and what requires time to verify.

heldForEditorialReview.title: How Sustainability Consultants Help Improve Your Supply Chain
heldForEditorialReview.subtitle: Supply-chain work becomes tractable when material exposure and commercial leverage determine where attention goes first.
heldForEditorialReview.author: Campbell Ohrlis
heldForEditorialReview.authorBio: Campbell Ohrlis works with leadership teams on the commercial question underneath sustainability: where exposure is material, what can be influenced, and which decision belongs first.
heldForEditorialReview.heroAlt: Container port and freight logistics infrastructure at dusk
heldForEditorialReview.excerpt: You do not control most of the supply chain. That is why materiality and leverage need to decide where you act first.
heldForEditorialReview.linkedInExcerpt: Supply-chain sustainability is not a survey problem. It is a prioritisation problem. Screen for material exposure and commercial leverage, then direct attention to the suppliers, lanes, contracts, and locations where a decision can change cost, resilience, and emissions together.

faq.question: What should a company prioritize first in supply-chain sustainability?
faq.answer: Start with material exposure and leverage. Look for suppliers, lanes, categories, or single-source dependencies that matter to spend, volume, operational criticality, emissions intensity, or physical risk, then assess whether a commercial action is possible.

faq.question: Can supply-chain action begin without complete supplier data?
faq.answer: Yes. Spend-based estimates and existing procurement, freight, and operational records can provide a useful first screen. Primary data is most valuable once the material working set is clear.

faq.question: Which supply-chain changes can affect both cost and emissions?
faq.answer: Freight mode and routing, load factor, packaging design, supplier energy intensity, sourcing concentration, contract terms, and joint improvement projects can each affect cost, resilience, and emissions. The right choice depends on the operating context.

faq.question: Why should contract and renewal dates be part of the analysis?

sections.content:
Everything that makes environmental decisions difficult inside your own four walls gets harder across a supply chain. You own less of the data, less of the equipment, and less of the decision. Costs, exposure, and emissions sit across suppliers, lanes, and facilities that belong to other businesses.

That is precisely why prioritisation matters. The job is not to send the same request to the whole supply base. It is to identify the suppliers, lanes, and contracts where a decision can change the outcome.
Why this is arriving on the leadership agenda now

Customer requirements are moving down supply chains. Large buyers in automotive, retail, food, and government increasingly ask suppliers to explain exposure, emissions, and improvement plans. A weak answer can become a revenue and relationship issue before it becomes a reporting issue.

Physical exposure is also material. CDP reported in May 2026 that 11,261 companies disclosing full environmental data through its 2025 questionnaire anticipated US$714 billion in future financial impacts from extreme weather. It attributed US$326 billion of that anticipated exposure to reduced production capacity, and reported that 48% of identified risks were expected within two years. These are system-level figures, not an individual-company forecast, but they make the business case for examining critical dependencies more concrete.

A 2024 Nature study led by researchers at King’s College London and Tsinghua University estimated that climate-disrupted global supply chains could add US$3.75 trillion to US$24.7 trillion in net economic losses in adjusted 2020 dollars by 2060, depending on the emissions pathway. The implication for an individual company is not to model the global number. It is to understand where its own dependencies are concentrated.

sections.content: The filter that makes the work tractable

Apply two questions to each supplier, category, and lane. First: is it material? Consider spend, volume, emissions intensity, production criticality, and exposure to disruption. Second: do you have leverage? Consider your share of the supplier’s revenue, the timing of the contract, viable alternatives, specifications, and what the supplier needs from the relationship.

Material exposure with leverage is where action belongs. Material exposure without leverage may call for alternatives, resilience planning, or a different sourcing strategy rather than another questionnaire. Exposure that is not material should not consume scarce operating attention. This filter gives procurement and operations a working set they can explain.
Where value often turns up

Freight mode, routing, consolidation, load factor, backhaul opportunities, and network design can affect cost and emissions together. Packaging can influence freight cost and material use, especially where specifications no longer match the product or route. Supplier energy intensity can be a sourcing, cost, and resilience signal when comparable production data is available.

Concentration and location risk can be equally important. A single-source component from a facility exposed to flooding or water stress is a resilience problem with a financial consequence. Contract terms and renewal calendars can be practical leverage points. Joint improvement projects can make sense where a long relationship and commercial leverage allow the parties to share a credible benefit.
Handle data honestly and in phases

Supplier-specific primary data is valuable, but many suppliers do not yet have it in a comparable form. Start with the procurement, freight, and operating records you already have. Use estimates for a broad first screen, label the confidence clearly, then seek better information from the suppliers and lanes that the materiality-and-leverage filter surfaced.

The first result should earn the access for the next round. A broad survey before the decision criteria are clear can create work without improving a decision. A phased approach directs deeper data collection to the places where it can change a sourcing, logistics, or contract choice.
Where AI helps, and where a human check still matters

Generative tools can accelerate supply-base mapping, lane screening, first-pass emissions estimation, and supplier-engagement drafts. That changes what is practical to analyse. It does not know whether an alternative supplier has a long qualification cycle, whether a mode shift breaks a service commitment, or whether a carrier’s regional capacity has changed.

Every draft needs a human sanity test before it reaches procurement. Speed matters. So does operating context.
What an early supply-chain decision phase should produce

A useful first phase produces a spend-and-exposure map that is good enough to rank rather than to report. It identifies a visible working set of material suppliers and lanes, names what was screened out, and recommends a next action with stated assumptions. It can also map contracts and renewals, and create a short list of concentrated dependencies that deserve attention.

The aim is not a complete inventory before action. It is a defensible first move that improves the next decision.
What to ask before you buy help

Ask which suppliers and lanes are material, what was screened out, and what can be learned before new supplier data arrives. Ask which changes may affect cost as well as emissions, where single-source exposure exists, who reviews the analysis before procurement sees it, and whether the advisor sells products, software, or referral arrangements.

The final question is what happens after the recommendation. Supply-chain change touches procurement, logistics, production, and suppliers at once. Someone has to hold the work together to done.
Your supply chain contains more opportunity than your own operations and less control. That combination makes choosing correctly matter more here than anywhere else.
Sources and context

Sources: CDP, “Extreme Weather Risk is Reshaping the Global Economy,” 12 May 2026; and Wang et al., “Global supply chains amplify economic costs of future extreme heat risk,” Nature, 2024. System-level figures are included for context and are not forecasts for an individual company.

sections.content:
Earth runs on nine systems that keep it stable. Scientists call them planetary boundaries. Together they mark the safe operating space for human civilisation. Stay inside it and the planet stays a dependable home. Step outside and the risks stack up.

We are now outside on seven of them. And every one of those seven is at its worst level on record.

That is the finding of the 2026 Planetary Health Check, recently released by the Planetary Boundaries Science Lab at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK). The seven breached boundaries are climate change, biosphere integrity, land system change, freshwater change, biogeochemical flows, novel entities and ocean acidification. Every one has worsened since tracking began in 2009. Only the ozone layer and aerosol loading remain in the safe zone.

The report's lead author, Boris Sakschewski, called the diagnosis unambiguous. His point was simple. The risk of lasting and possibly irreversible change keeps rising. Our margin for error keeps shrinking.
A year of extremes

We don't need a report to feel this. The last 12 months made it plain.

Pakistan's 2025 monsoon floods affected more than 6.9 million people. Ocean heat hit a new record and helped Hurricane Melissa grow into a Category 5 storm before it struck Jamaica. Heat stress bleached about 84% of the world's coral reef area, the largest event ever recorded.

This summer, Western Europe had its hottest June and July on record. Drought hit France, Spain, Germany and the UK. Wildfires burned across Europe and in Canada and the US. Japan, South Korea and parts of the Middle East saw record heat.

Carbon dioxide in the air reached an all-time high of 426 parts per million. Many scientists put the safe limit at 350. Before the industrial revolution it was 280.
Disturbing trend

The report raises a new worry. Forests and soils absorb a large share of the carbon we emit. These natural carbon sinks may be weakening under repeated heat, drought and fire. The issue? The models may be overestimating how much carbon they can absorb going forward. It’s a similar story with our oceans, which absorb a larger share of carbon emissions than our forests and soils combined.

This matters for every net zero plan on the books. Most people assume these natural sinks will just continue to keep working. If they falter, the carbon emission reduction work left for humans gets bigger and the timeline gets shorter.

Planetary boundaries don't happen in isolation. Levke Caesar, the lab's lead researcher, put it well. "We are not pushing seven independent systems beyond their safe ranges; we are changing several parts of one connected system at the same time."
Customers are feeling the pain

For business, testing planetary boundaries is not abstract, but carries real weight. Companies reporting to CDP anticipate a $714 billion hit from extreme weather, with nearly half of the losses expected within two years.
There’s good news

The situation isn’t hopeless. The ozone layer is healing because the world acted together. PIK director Johan Rockström said it clearly. "We do not have the luxury of time, but we do have the knowledge, capacity and solutions to change course."
The real barrier is complexity

Customers are a key to addressing planetary boundaries. They need to up their game. The problem is not a lack of attractive solutions in the marketplace. Rather it is too slow a rate of customer adoption of the best of these solutions.

Over the past decade or two, hundreds of billions of dollars and a large amount of human ingenuity have gone into solving sustainability problems. It’s not surprising that this has resulted in an explosion of great solutions. Unfortunately, the associated complexity causes confusion greatly slowing customer decision making and reducing the quality of decisions they ultimately make.

To take maximum advantage of the smorgasbord of sustainability products, services and software solutions available today, customers need to be able to do the right sustainable things in the right order with the right vendors at speed. Unfortunately, they cannot do this because they lack the data, software and expertise required to do so. As a result, dramatically suboptimal sustainability results are the norm.
How Enduring Advantage helps

Enduring Advantage exists to answer one question for its customer: “Out of all the sustainability solutions the customer could implement next, which should it implement? Which solution will give it the biggest bang for its buck?” The selected solution is implemented and then the exercise is repeated in a continuous improvement process we call The Next Best Thing (NBT).

Returns from sustainability initiatives can come in surprising ways. For example, CDP global disclosure data suggests that pre-emptive measures to mitigate the $714 billion in extreme weather damages customers expect to experience in the future (over $350 billion in the next 2 years) could reduce their total costs by roughly 13 times compared to simply absorbing the damages and associated losses. This means that the NBT could easily be spending money to protect against an adverse outcome.

The NBT selection process only includes initiatives that have a positive environmental impact. This is a necessary condition for consideration. The NBT is the environmentally beneficial initiative that yields the best financial return to the customer.

The NBT process ensures that the customer does the right things in the right order with the right vendors at speed thereby ensuring the best possible financial and environmental results over time. Enduring Advantage can do this because, unlike its customers, it has the data, software and expertise required to do it.

We sit on our customers’ side of the table helping them quickly prioritize the supply options available to them to ensure they get the best possible sustainability results over the shortest possible time frame.

Enduring Advantage helps customers dramatically improve their environmental AND financial performance.
The Right Things in the Right Order, With the Right Vendors, At Speed.
